blocks.text: About this site
A personal project of Rabbi Daniel Bogard: why it exists, where its information comes from, and how to correct it.
It grew out of my election classes. It is my own project, independent of my congregation.
The purpose is education. The site explains the choices on the ballot, what voters say matters to them, and whose lives are affected without having a vote. It does not endorse a party.
Sources and perspective

Numbers carry dates and sources. Survey findings identify the population surveyed; a finding about Jewish respondents is not presented as a finding about all Israelis. Party positions are attributed to the parties, with links to their statements or reporting of their answers.

Sources have different purposes and perspectives. The [Israel Democracy Institute](https://en.idi.org.il/about/about-idi/) describes itself as nonpartisan and committed to strengthening Israeli democracy. [Peace Now](https://peacenow.org.il/en/about-us) advocates a two-state agreement and opposes settlement expansion. Their evidence is assessed alongside their methods and stated purposes. Advocacy- or party-sponsored surveys are used only when they provide otherwise unavailable evidence, with the sponsor identified.

My decisions about terminology are [documented openly](https://github.com/RavBogard/israelielection/blob/main/docs/research/RULINGS.md). Claims, legal findings and political positions are attributed to their sources. I take responsibility for the site’s framing and language.
How the polls work

New polls are imported from Wikipedia’s election-polling tables, retaining links to the underlying reports where available. Automated checks flag inconsistent seat totals, unknown parties, duplicate entries, date problems and unusually large changes. Polls that fail those checks go to review.

The current average uses each publisher’s latest campaign poll within 14 days of the newest poll. Larger samples receive more weight, using the square root of sample size. When sample size is unavailable, the calculation uses the median known sample size in that set.

Each list’s seat average uses only polls where it passes the electoral threshold; the site also shows how often it passes. Lists passing in fewer than half the polls that report them are excluded from the Coalition Builder’s default total. When these averages add to more than 120, coalition calculations scale them down proportionally. The [Polls page](/polls) shows the unscaled figures.
The main average includes Channel 14. An alternative omits Channel 14 and i24NEWS, allowing readers to see how those pollsters affect the picture. Polls are estimates, not election results.
News, development and checking
Headlines are fetched automatically from news outlets’ feeds. Gemini Flash 3.8 writes the daily briefing from those headlines and summaries, with source links for every sentence.

It publishes automatically after checks for valid source references and a basic match between the sentence and its cited material. Those checks do not establish that every claim is correct. There is no routine human review before publication; I can correct or remove a briefing.

Site development is primarily done through Claude Code using Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. Reference pages underwent separate fact-checking rounds against cited sources, with verification records kept in the repository.
Reuse

The site’s original text is licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). You may share and adapt it for noncommercial use, giving credit, linking the license and indicating changes.
Privacy

This site uses Google Analytics to understand visits and page use. Google Analytics uses cookies and collects information about page visits, browsers and devices, and approximate location. Read [how Google collects and processes this information](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/6004245). Google also offers an [Analytics opt-out browser add-on](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout) for supported browsers.

Reading suggestions are off by default. If you turn them on, this browser stores known public page identifiers and reading times for up to 30 days. They are used to suggest related reading, not to infer political affiliation or reorder the main headlines and evidence. You can reset the reading history, or turn suggestions off and erase it, from the Suggested reading controls. This history is not an email subscription.

Where email updates are available, a separate opt-in and confirmation are required. The service stores your verified email address, selected language and topics, confirmation and consent records, and delivery or suppression records needed to manage the subscription. Private links let you change preferences or unsubscribe. Unsubscribing stops future subscription messages; it does not promise deletion of every delivery, consent or suppression record. Confirmation and preference pages exclude analytics and use a no-referrer policy. Do not share their private links.
Corrections

Please [report a correction](/corrections#report) by email draft or by [GitHub issue](https://github.com/RavBogard/israelielection/issues); both are offered there. Material changes, such as updates to the count, are logged on [changes and evidence](/changes). Include the page address, the wording or number in question, and a supporting source where possible.
—Rabbi Daniel Bogard
The American lens
What Americans most often get wrong: Palestinian statehood and the conduct of the war in Gaza are not top-tier issues for most Jewish Israeli voters.

The thing Americans most often get wrong about Israel's election is what it is about. In the United States, the conduct of the war in Gaza and a Palestinian state are at the center of the argument over Israel. In Israel's 2026 campaign, for most Jewish voters and for the Jewish-majority parties, they were not. This page starts there, then sets out where the rest of the American map (pro-Israel and its critics, left and right, religious and secular) fits and where it misleads.
What the election is not about

For most Jewish Israeli voters, and for the Jewish-majority lists on the October 27, 2026 ballot, the Palestinian question was not a top-tier issue in 2026. That question takes in Palestinian rights and statehood, two states or one, equality, Israel's military rule over the West Bank, which it has occupied since 1967 ([Times of Israel, July 19, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/world-court-israeli-presence-in-east-jerusalem-west-bank-is-illegal-and-must-end/)), and the conduct of the war in Gaza.

**What voters said would decide their vote.** Asked by the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) for their first and second considerations, Jewish respondents chose foreign affairs and security (39%), the economy and cost of living (38%) and conscription (27%). The Palestinian issue was not offered as a separate answer ([IDI, Aug 31–Sept 3, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)).
<Chart id="american-lens.vote-considerations" />

**What the parties say.** Only Ra'am and the Joint List name a Palestinian state as a goal. In a Ynet questionnaire no Jewish-majority list did: several oppose one, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! says it is "not on the agenda," The Democrats speak of "separation," and Likud declined to answer ([Ynet, Sept 30, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/h1dpvu9cgl)). Western recognitions of the State of Palestine in September 2025 united the main Jewish-majority parties against them: Yair Lapid called the step "a reward for terror," and Yair Golan of The Democrats "destructive" ([Times of Israel, Sept 22, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-unites-against-hollow-palestine-recognition-but-pm-could-go-too-far/)). Netanyahu uses the idea against rivals; his video of September 18 asked, "Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?", aimed at Eisenkot, whom Reuters describes as "a hawkish former military chief" ([Reuters, via Jerusalem Post, Sept 29, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-910068)).

**Where the question is on the ballot.** Ra'am supports a negotiated two-state solution (Ynet). Yousef Jabareen, who leads Hadash and the Joint List, has said the list would push for renewed negotiations with the Palestinian leadership toward a Palestinian state alongside Israel, and seek equality for Arab citizens ([Jerusalem Post, Sept 1, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-907154)). The Joint List's answer to Ynet calls the settlements a violation of international law and a war crime. The Palestinians whose statehood is the question have no vote for the Knesset: most in East Jerusalem are Israeli residents, not citizens, and those in the rest of the West Bank and in Gaza are not Israeli citizens either ([Inter-Agency Task Force, updated Dec 2022](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf)); see [who votes](/how-it-works/who-votes).

**What Jewish Israelis say about Gaza and a state.** In July 2025 the IDI asked, "To what extent are you personally troubled or not troubled by the reports of famine and suffering among the Palestinian population in Gaza?" Of Jewish respondents, 79% said they were not so troubled or not at all troubled; 86% of Arab respondents said they were troubled ([IDI, July 27–31, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/60357)). In spring 2026, 16% of Jewish Israelis thought a way could be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully, and 64% said it could not ([Pew, April 5–May 6, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/09/pg_2026.09.15_coexistence_report.pdf)).
**Why, in pollsters' words.** "To many Jewish Israelis, the recent war in Gaza is evidence that peaceful coexistence is not an option," Pew reported. One respondent put it this way:
A Jewish Israeli man, 36. Pew survey respondent. Pew Research Center. https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/09/pg_2026.09.15_coexistence_report.pdf. Sept 15, 2026
Since what happened on Oct. 7, I have lost all faith in the Palestinian people and in the two-state solution for both peoples.

The share of Jewish Israelis who thought coexistence possible was 32% in spring 2023, before October 7, and 16% in 2025 and 2026 ([Pew, Sept 15, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/09/pg_2026.09.15_coexistence_report.pdf)). In 2026, 68% of Jewish respondents told the IDI that October 7 is a central factor in their vote ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)). Asked Pew's coexistence question, Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem were about as doubtful: 21% said a way can be found and 68% said it cannot. Many of them, Pew reported, "say coexistence is not an option while they live under Israeli control" ([Pew, March 30–April 28, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/15/many-israelis-and-palestinians-say-they-cannot-coexist-peacefully-and-explain-why/)).

**The legal record.** Much of the American argument draws on a legal record that Israel rejects: South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice, which has not been decided; the International Criminal Court's November 2024 arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant; and a UN commission of inquiry's September 2025 conclusion. [Who votes, and who doesn't](/how-it-works/who-votes) sets out each finding in its own words, with Israel's response.

**The American contrast.** In the United States the war is where the argument over Israel happens. In a Washington Post poll of 815 American Jews in September 2025, 61% said Israel has committed war crimes against Palestinians ([Washington Post poll, Sept 2–9, 2025, via JTA](https://www.jta.org/2025/10/06/united-states/poll-40-of-american-jews-believe-israel-is-committing-genocide-in-gaza)). In May 2026, Americans viewed the Palestinian people (50% favorable) about as favorably as the Israeli people (52%) ([Pew, May 4–17, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/07/09/americans-views-of-israelis-have-grown-increasingly-negative-but-views-of-palestinians-have-held-fairly-steady/)). See [a Palestinian state and the 2026 vote](/issues/palestinian-state) for the party table.
Why "pro-Israel" is not an Israeli category
The best-known American organizations on Israel each define themselves in American terms: by the U.S. policy they want, or by the American Jews they organize.

- **AIPAC:** "AIPAC is an American grassroots organization that works to strengthen the U.S.-Israel partnership" ([AIPAC, About](https://www.aipac.org/about)).
- **J Street:** "J Street organizes pro-Israel, pro-peace, pro-democracy Americans to promote US policies" ([J Street, About](https://jstreet.org/about-us/)).
- **Jewish Voice for Peace:** "The Jewish Voice for Peace family of organizations organizes a grassroots, multiracial, cross-class, intergenerational movement of U.S. Jews into solidarity with the Palestinian freedom struggle" ([JVP, About](https://www.jewishvoiceforpeace.org/about/)).

All three organize Americans and work on American policy and politics, not on Knesset elections. "Pro-Israel," in the sense these groups argue over, is a position in American politics about American policy. Israeli voters are not choosing between pro-Israel and anti-Israel parties.

American views of Israel also divide along American lines of religion and party. In March 2026, 64% of Jewish Americans and 65% of White evangelical Protestants viewed Israel favorably, against 37% of all Americans, down from 55% in 2022. Republicans were 58% favorable; 80% of Democrats were unfavorable ([Pew Research Center, March 23–29, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/07/negative-views-of-israel-netanyahu-continue-to-rise-among-americans-especially-young-people/)).
Why Israeli left and right don't line up with American ones

**The main axis is the Palestinian question, not the economy.** An expert survey of Israeli party positions in the 2021 and 2022 elections found that the general left-right dimension is "overwhelmed by parties' positions on policies related to the Arab-Israeli conflict" ([Zur and Bakker, *Party Politics*, CHES-Israel 2021–22](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/13540688231218917)). Economic positions are a separate, weaker dimension. The same study places Shas and United Torah Judaism, the two Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, on the right on the West Bank and a Palestinian state, and on the left on economics.

**Group identity predicts the vote better than income.** A study of Israel's 2020 locality results found that "voting behavior is better explained by affiliation to the social group" than by education, income or place ([Zeedan, *Societies*, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4698/14/9/177)). In the March 2021 election, 46% of Likud voters reported below-average household income and 29% above-average; 46% of Yesh Atid voters reported above-average income ([IDI, six pooled polls, n=3,948, 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/39409)).

**"Left" and "right" track the Palestinian question.** In spring 2025, 54% of Israelis on the left and 7% on the right thought Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully ([Pew, 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2025/06/03/views-of-the-potential-for-lasting-peace/)). Israeli Jews have also moved right on their own placement: 62% put themselves on the right in 2022, up from 46% in 2019.
<Chart id="american-lens.self-placement" />
Where the fights rhyme and where they don't

**Courts.** Both countries argue over how far courts should check elected majorities, and who picks the judges. On January 1, 2024, a full 15-justice panel struck down the 2023 law ending "reasonableness" review, 8–7 ([NPR, January 1, 2024](https://www.npr.org/2024/01/01/1222400537/israel-supreme-court-ruling-judiciary-changes)). Judges are chosen by a nine-member committee of ministers, lawmakers, lawyers and justices, not nominated by an executive and confirmed by a legislature. A 2025 law changes that committee and takes effect when the next Knesset convenes, after the October 27, 2026 vote ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/regime-change-high-court-tears-into-coalition-bid-to-control-judicial-appointments/)). See [courts and the judicial overhaul](/issues/courts).

**Religion and state.** "Israel does not allow civil marriage, and Jewish marriages conducted in Israel must be sanctioned by Orthodox rabbis" ([Pew, 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). And the Israeli liberal camp is mostly secular, not Reform or Conservative: in Pew's surveys, 3% of Israeli Jews identified as Reform and 2% as Conservative, against 35% and 18% of U.S. Jews ([Pew, 2016; Israel data 2014–15, U.S. data 2013](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/comparisons-between-jews-in-israel-and-the-u-s/)). See [religion and state](/issues/religion-state).
The data on the gap
On the question Pew has asked both publics, Israeli Jews moved; American Jews, up to 2020, did not.
<Chart id="american-lens.coexist-jews" />
<Chart id="american-lens.coexist-israelis" />

Where the same questions go to both publics, American Jews are more worried and Israeli Jews more confident. The Jewish People Policy Institute's U.S. sample is a panel of "connected" Jews, more engaged than American Jews as a whole.

Misreadings

**"The election is a referendum on the war in Gaza, or on two states."** Jewish voters rank security, the cost of living and conscription highest, and IDI did not offer the Palestinian issue as an answer ([IDI, Aug 31–Sept 3, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)). A Palestinian state was on the ballot mainly through the Joint List and Ra'am. See [a Palestinian state and the 2026 vote](/issues/palestinian-state).

**"Arab citizens don't really take part."** Palestinian citizens of Israel vote and win seats: in 2022, Ra'am won 5 and Hadash–Ta'al 5, while Balad fell short of the 3.25% threshold with 2.9% ([IDI, 2022 results](https://en.idi.org.il/israeli-elections-and-parties/elections/2022/)). See [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens).

**"American Jews are Israel's strongest supporters in America."** In March 2026, Jewish Americans (64% favorable) were about where White evangelical Protestants were (65%) ([Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/07/negative-views-of-israel-netanyahu-continue-to-rise-among-americans-especially-young-people/)).
Druze
A small, Arabic-speaking religious community whose men are drafted: its size, how its villages have voted since 2019, its views on the issues, and the Golan Druze.

The Druze are an Arabic-speaking religious community, most of whom live in villages on Mount Carmel and in the Galilee. Statistics usually place them among Israel's Arab citizens. The Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) counts them inside its "Arab" population group, where they made up 7.4% at the end of 2022 ([CBS, April 2023](https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/Society_&_Culture/druze-stats2023.pdf)). In a 2014–15 survey, 71% of Druze said they are ethnically Arab, against 99% of Muslims and 96% of Christians ([Pew Research Center, March 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). Asked which part of their identity matters most, most name something else. In May 2026, 64.8% of Druze respondents named Israeli citizenship as the most important component of their identity ([Konrad Adenauer Program, Tel Aviv University, May 2026](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)). In an older IDI survey (May 2016), in which Druze were about 12% of 362 Arab respondents, 54% named their religious identity, 37% Israeli, 5% Arab, and none Palestinian ([IDI, May 2016](https://www.idi.org.il/media/8292/)). Unlike Muslim and Christian Arab citizens, Druze men are drafted. This page treats the Druze as a group of their own. The [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens) page covers Muslims and Christians.
Size, growth and geography

CBS counted about 150,000 Druze at the end of 2022, 1.6% of Israel's population ([CBS, April 2023](https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/Society_&_Culture/druze-stats2023.pdf)). That count includes the Druze of the Golan Heights, and the release does not give a figure without them. They are covered in the box at the end of this page and left out of the figures that follow wherever the source allows. In 2021, about 81% of Druze lived in the Northern District and 19% in the Haifa District. The largest communities were Daliyat al-Karmel (17,500), Yarka (17,300) and Maghar (13,500). The median age was 29.6 at the end of 2021. Fertility has fallen from 7.92 children per woman in 1964 to 2.00 in 2021, and the growth rate was 1.2% that year (same source).

The Carmel villages are Daliyat al-Karmel and Isfiya. The Galilee villages include Yarka, Julis, the seat of the spiritual leadership, Beit Jann, Hurfeish, Kisra-Sumei, Yanuh-Jat, Sajur, Ein al-Asad and Peki'in. Druze also live in mixed towns such as Maghar, Abu Snan, Rameh and Shefa-Amr. In 2022 the employment rate was 50.8%, against 42.6% among Muslims and 68.7% among Christians, and 14.8% of adults held an academic degree ([CBS](https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/Society_&_Culture/druze-stats2023.pdf)).

Druze men have been conscripted since 1956 ([Zeidan Atashi, former Druze MK, via Jewish Virtual Library](https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/druze-in-israel-and-the-question-of-compulsory-military-service)). No primary IDF enlistment rate was found. In Pew's 2014–15 survey, about six in ten Druze men had served (45%) or were serving (15%) ([Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/03/21/5-facts-about-israeli-druze-a-unique-religious-and-ethnic-group/)).
How their villages have voted, 2019–2022

The figures below add up the ten localities that a Moshe Dayan Center study treats as at least 95% Druze ([Shanan and Ilat, 2021](https://dayan.org/he/content/5714)): Daliyat al-Karmel, Yarka, Beit Jann, Hurfeish, Kisra-Sumei, Yanuh-Jat, Peki'in, Julis, Sajur and Ein al-Asad. They leave out Isfiya and the mixed towns, whose results cannot be read as Druze votes, and the Golan villages.
<Chart id="druze.vote" />

The vote goes overwhelmingly to the parties IDI classes as Zionist, about 90% in 2022 ([IDI, December 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47986)), but it is not a vote for the right. In 2022, Likud, Religious Zionism, Shas and United Torah Judaism together took about 13% in the ten villages. Most of the rest went to opposition parties ([CEC, computed](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)).

The vote follows the home villages of Druze candidates. In 2022, Beit Jann gave Meretz 61.6%; Ali Salalha, Meretz's no. 4, is from Beit Jann. Daliyat al-Karmel gave National Unity 54.9%; Akram Hasson, its no. 16, lives there ([CEC, computed](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). The Dayan Center study, covering 1996 to 2020, found the same pattern: "nearly every party that placed a Druze candidate in a realistic spot won the most support in his village" ([Shanan and Ilat, 2021, translated from Hebrew](https://dayan.org/he/content/5714)).
Turnout has fallen from 76.8% in 1996 ([Dayan Center](https://dayan.org/he/content/5714)) to 50.8% in 2022, well below the national rate.
<Chart id="druze.turnout" />

Only one Druze member of Knesset was elected in 2022, Hamad Amar of Yisrael Beiteinu. IDI called it "an all-time low" ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47986)). For 2026, Ali Salalha finished 18th in the Democrats' primary ([Ynetnews, July 20, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/synmdasnzx)). A Druze party, Brit Achim, was launched in May 2026 by Wajdi Sarhan, a reserve officer ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/former-idf-commander-wajdi-sarhan-launches-first-druze-political-party-in-decades/)). In September Sarhan announced he would not run, saying that with the small parties "the conditions for a joint and equal run agreement were not created" ([Ynetnews, September 8, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/bfi2ue5qp)).
What they think on the issues

No large Druze-only survey exists. In IDI's Democracy Index 2025 (fieldwork May 4–28, 2025), Druze were about 8.4% of 364 Arab respondents, roughly 31 people. IDI itself limited its use of the religion breakdown for that reason ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). The figures below are a rough guide only. No 2026 survey breaks out Druze views on any of the issues.
<Chart id="druze.idi-2025" />
**[The Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft).** IDI 2025 gives no Druze breakdown. The community's own draft is described above.

**[Courts](/issues/courts).** Druze trust the Supreme Court more than Muslims or Christians do (61%). They are also the most likely of the three groups to say it intervenes too much (71%). 83.5% support a constitution ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

**[War and hostages](/issues/war-hostages).** Trust in the IDF rose from 64% in 2024 to 84% in 2025, about the Jewish level (83.5%). Two-thirds (67%) say the state provides security for its citizens, and 81% are optimistic about Israel's future (same source). No sourced total of Druze soldiers killed since October 7, 2023 was found.

**[West Bank](/issues/west-bank).** The only Druze figure found is old: in 2014–15, 66% said settlements hurt Israel's security ([Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)).
**[Religion and state](/issues/religion-state).** No Druze poll on the 2018 Nation-State Law was found. The evidence is how the community acted (below).

**[Economy](/issues/economy).** 58% say the state manages to ensure citizens' welfare, against 31–32% of Muslims and Christians. But only 29% trust the government and 19% trust the Knesset ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).
Who they are

The Druze spiritual leader since 1993 has been Sheikh Mowafaq Tarif ([Moment, February 2018](https://momentmag.com/interview-sheik-mowafaq-tafik-spiritual-leader-israeli-druze/)), born in Julis, who succeeded his grandfather, Sheikh Amin Tarif ([University of Haifa](https://rlgslsb.haifa.ac.il/en/2025/02/sheikh-mowafaq-tarif/)). Jewish-Israeli leaders have called the bond a "blood covenant," *brit damim*. Sephardi Chief Rabbi David Yosef, visiting Julis in August 2025, said: "We have a blood covenant with the Druze community, and the state must do everything to protect the Druze wherever they are" ([Times of Israel, August 28, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/chief-rabbi-stresses-blood-covenant-with-druze-brethren-in-meeting-of-religious-leaders/)). The Druze speakers quoted here use other words: loyalty, sacrifice, equality.
The 2018 Nation-State Law tested that bond. On July 25, 2018, about 100 Druze reserve officers protested it ([Ynetnews](https://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-5316576,00.html)).
Brig. Gen. (res.) Amal As'ad. Ynetnews. https://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-5316576,00.html. July 25, 2018
After we built this home together with the Jews, the Nationality Law excludes the Druze community from that home and put it outside the fence.

On August 4, 2018, some 90,000 Druze, with other opponents of the law, filled Rabin Square, by Ynet's estimate ([Ynet](https://www.ynet.co.il/articles/0,7340,L-5322446,00.html)). Sheikh Tarif told the rally:
Sheikh Mowafaq Tarif. Druze spiritual leader. Ynet (translated from Hebrew). https://www.ynet.co.il/articles/0,7340,L-5322446,00.html. August 4, 2018
Despite our unreserved loyalty to the state, the state does not see us as equals.

From July 13, 2025, clashes in Suwayda in southern Syria pitted "Druze fighters against Sunni Bedouin tribes and the army and its allies" ([France 24, July 17, 2025](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20250717-death-toll-from-syria-clashes-rises-to-594-after-days-of-sectarian-violence)). The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria reported in March 2026 that more than 1,700 people were killed and nearly 200,000 displaced, in violations "mainly against the Druze and Bedouin communities" by actors including government forces and Druze armed groups. It found that after government forces withdrew, "Druze armed groups then attacked Bedouin civilians" ([UN News, March 27, 2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/03/1167210)). Israel struck Syrian government forces in Suwayda, and dozens of Israeli civilians crossed the border near Majdal Shams ([Ynetnews, July 15, 2025](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/by11g11e4ull)). Hamad Amar said: "The prime minister and defense minister have repeatedly promised to protect our brethren across the border" (same source).

About 26,000–29,000 Druze live in four villages in the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights: Majdal Shams, Mas'ade, Buq'ata and Ein Qiniyye ([Times of Israel, January 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/taboo-no-more-one-in-five-golan-druze-now-holds-israeli-citizenship/); [March 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/after-years-of-hesitation-more-druze-of-the-golan-heights-seek-israeli-citizenship/)). Israel annexed the Golan under Israeli law in 1981. Most residents hold permanent residency, not citizenship, and only citizens vote for the Knesset. They are not counted in this page's vote figures.

At the end of 2024, about 6,000 held citizenship, roughly one in five ([Times of Israel, January 6, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/taboo-no-more-one-in-five-golan-druze-now-holds-israeli-citizenship/)). Applications numbered 438 in 2022 and 406 in 2023 (same source), then surged to 3,750 in 2025. By March 2026 about 38% of Majdal Shams residents and 37–43% in the other villages held citizenship ([Times of Israel, March 15, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/after-years-of-hesitation-more-druze-of-the-golan-heights-seek-israeli-citizenship/)).

In 2022 the four villages had 2,755 registered voters, and 23.2% voted: Yesh Atid 24.3%, National Unity 19.4%, Likud 15.5%, Yisrael Beiteinu 15.5% ([CEC, computed](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). The 2026 roll had not been published when this page was checked, and it was expected to be larger.

On July 27, 2024, a rocket, which Israel said Hezbollah fired and Hezbollah denied, struck a soccer field in Majdal Shams and killed 12 Golan Druze children. Council head Dolan Abu Saleh, four of whose relatives were among the dead, said: "All of the Majdal Shams family lean towards peace. We do not want war or retribution" ([The National, July 30, 2024](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2024/07/31/majdal-shams-residents-golan-heights/)).
Ethiopian-Israelis
A short profile of Israelis of Ethiopian origin: how many, where they live, what the thin vote evidence shows, and how policing has figured in their politics.
Size, growth and geography

At the end of 2024, 177,600 Israelis were of Ethiopian origin ([CBS, reported by JNS, November 2025](https://www.jns.org/israels-jewish-ethiopian-population-reached-177600-in-2024/)). The Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) counts people born in Ethiopia and Israeli-born children of Ethiopian-born fathers. A growing share were born in Israel.
<Chart id="ethiopian-israelis.population" />

No town has an Ethiopian-Israeli majority. The highest share is in Kiryat Malachi, 13.9% of residents; the largest numbers are in Netanya (12,900), Beersheba (10,600) and Petah Tikva (10,100), all at the end of 2023 ([CBS, 2024](https://www.cbs.gov.il/he/mediarelease/DocLib/2024/371/11_24_371b.pdf)). Between 1,680 and 1,812 people a year came from Ethiopia in 2021–23 (same source). More than 7,000 people of Ethiopian Jewish descent were still waiting in Gondar and Addis Ababa in September 2025, many with close family in Israel; some are labeled Beta Israel and others Falash Mura ([Shmuel Legesse, Jerusalem Post op-ed, September 2025](https://www.jpost.com/opinion/article-867319)).

Gaps in schooling and income remain. In 2022/23, 77.7% of Ethiopian-origin 12th-graders were eligible for a matriculation (bagrut) certificate, against 85.6% in Hebrew-language education. In the 2022 household survey, net household income was about 20% below the general population (NIS 14,676 against 18,237 a month) and spending per person about 40% lower ([CBS, 2024](https://www.cbs.gov.il/he/mediarelease/DocLib/2024/371/11_24_371b.pdf)).
How their towns have voted

Results are reported by place, and no place is mostly Ethiopian-Israeli. The closest evidence is a press analysis of polling stations in Ethiopian-Israeli neighborhoods before and after the 2019 protests over the Tekah shooting (below). It shows how these polling stations voted, not how Ethiopian-Israelis voted.
<Chart id="ethiopian-israelis.stations-2019" />

Likud fell 10 to 11 points at each station and Blue and White gained 9 to 15 ([Ynet, September 2019](https://www.ynet.co.il/articles/0,7340,L-5591507,00.html)). By March 2020 the shift had partly reversed: Blue and White fell to 18.5% at Ramat Eliyahu stations and 20.1% in Rehovot, and a community activist said many people he knew had gone back to Likud ([Ynet, March 2020](https://www.ynet.co.il/articles/0,7340,L-5688315,00.html)). Kiryat Malachi, the town with the largest Ethiopian-Israeli share, moved the same way.
<Chart id="ethiopian-israelis.kiryat-malachi" />
This page stops at 2020. No station-level analysis was found for 2021 or 2022, and whole-town results say little about a group that is at most a seventh of any town's residents.
What they think on the issues

No survey breaks out Ethiopian-Israelis on the Haredi draft, the courts, the war and the hostages, the West Bank, religion and state, or the economy, in 2026 or earlier. The samples are too small: in the Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 Democracy Index, 0.6% of the 1,205-person Jewish sample gave Ethiopian as their ethnicity, about seven people ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). The income figures above are the nearest measure on the economy. In a 2012 survey of immigrants who arrived from 1979 to 1991, almost all said they felt at home in Israel, and about a third reported personal discrimination at work and in the army ([Myers-JDC-Brookdale, 2012, the only such survey found](https://brookdale.jdc.org.il/en/publication/twenty-years-later-survey-ethiopian-immigrants-lived-israel-two-decades/)).
Who they are

Policing has been at the center of the community's protests. In 2019 a police officer's warning shot at the ground ricocheted and killed Solomon Tekah, 18. The officer was acquitted by the Haifa Magistrate's Court on April 2, 2024, on grounds of self-defense ([Times of Israel, April 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/police-officer-in-solomon-tekah-slaying-acquitted-of-negligent-manslaughter/)). "We had a small hope and it was dashed. There is no justice," his mother said. Police internal investigators appealed in May 2024 ([Times of Israel, May 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/police-investigators-appeal-acquittal-of-officer-in-killing-of-ethiopian-israeli-teen/)); no outcome was found.

When the community arrived in the 1980s, the Rabbinate required a symbolic renewal of their Jewish identity by ritual immersion, which no one argued was a conversion; many in the community saw it as humiliating and unnecessary, and the practice ended in 1985 after a month-long strike ([Atira Winchester, My Jewish Learning](https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/ethiopian-jews-in-israel/)).

Older voters have leaned to Likud; younger voters, focused on how police treat them, have been readier to move ([Times of Israel, March 2020](https://www.timesofisrael.com/in-southern-likud-stronghold-young-ethiopians-lose-patience-with-status-quo/)).
Avi Yossef. Voter, 35. Times of Israel. https://www.timesofisrael.com/seeking-likud-ouster-and-racial-equality-mk-highlights-ethiopian-israeli-shift/. 2020-02-24
Usually we vote for Likud because it's the party that brought Ethiopians back to Israel. But in the last election, we voted for Blue and White.
Karen. Blue and White voter, Kiryat Malachi. Times of Israel. https://www.timesofisrael.com/in-southern-likud-stronghold-young-ethiopians-lose-patience-with-status-quo/. 2020-03-02
We want a party that will truly represent us. Pnina has come to every one of our protests, so for me that party is Blue and White.

"Pnina" is MK Pnina Tamano-Shata, who said that year: "There are more Ethiopians in prison, more police brutality against us, higher poverty and a higher suicide rate" ([Times of Israel, February 2020](https://www.timesofisrael.com/seeking-likud-ouster-and-racial-equality-mk-highlights-ethiopian-israeli-shift/)).
Haredim
Israel's fastest-growing Jewish community, Ashkenazi and Sephardi: its size and streams, how its towns have voted, what it thinks on the issues, and the draft fight.
Size, growth and geography

Haredim (singular Haredi), often called ultra-Orthodox in English, are Israel's most strictly religious Jewish community, with their own school systems and their own parties. In Central Bureau of Statistics figures for 2025, released in September 2026, 11.5% of Jewish adults described themselves as Haredi ([CBS via Ynet, Sept 2026](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/sjc9lpcufl)). Because the community is very young, its share of the whole population is larger than its share of adults.

The Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 yearbook counts 1,452,350 Haredim, 14.3% of Israel's population, up from about 750,000 in 2009 ([IDI, Dec 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30207/final-final-haredi-shnaton-2025-pdf.pdf)). The Haredi Institute for Public Affairs, a Haredi-run research body, counts about 1.26 million, 12.5% of the population and 16% of Jews, at the end of 2024 ([Haredi Institute, 2025](https://machon.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/english-digital-1-1-1.pdf)). The counts define membership differently; both show the share rising.

The community grows by about 4.2% a year, and 57% of Haredim are under 20, against 31% of the general population. Fertility has fallen from 7.5 births per woman in 2003–05 to 6.5 in 2021–23, still about three times the rate among other Jewish women (2.2) ([IDI, Dec 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30207/final-final-haredi-shnaton-2025-pdf.pdf)).

Projections differ. A CBS projection cited by IDI has Haredim at about 20% of the population by 2040 and 24.4% by 2050; IDI's own estimate for 2050 is about 22% ([IDI, Feb 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63385)). An older CBS projection, from 2017, put the share at 32% by 2065 ([Israel National News, May 2017](https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/229972)). The Haredi Institute's 2065 scenarios range from 17.7%, if fertility falls substantially, to 22.6%, if it stays at its 2022 level ([Haredi Institute, 2025](https://machon.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/english-digital-1-1-1.pdf)).

The community is not one bloc. By the Haredi Institute's count, about a third are Sephardi and the rest belong to Ashkenazi streams: the Lithuanian (Litvish) stream, meaning non-Hasidic Ashkenazi Haredim, and the Hasidic courts, with Chabad counted separately.
<Chart id="haredim.streams" />

The streams map loosely onto parties. United Torah Judaism (UTJ) joins Agudat Yisrael, the Hasidic party, and Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian one ([Davar, Sept 2026](https://www.davar1.co.il/696518/); [UTJ](/parties/utj)). Shas, the Sephardi Haredi party, is a Haredi-led party with a traditional base: many of its voters are not Haredi ([Shas](/parties/shas); see [Masorti Israel](/communities/masorti)).

Most Haredim live in a handful of cities. In 2023 Jerusalem held 22.6% of all Haredim, Bnei Brak 15.6%, and the four "satellite" cities (Beit Shemesh, Modi'in Illit, Beitar Illit and Elad) 25% ([IDI, Dec 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30207/final-final-haredi-shnaton-2025-pdf.pdf)).
<Chart id="haredim.cities" />

Two of the largest, Modi'in Illit and Beitar Illit, are settlements, Haredi cities in the West Bank. Their residents are counted in settler population totals (see [Settlers](/communities/settlers)). Over the past decade, about 75,000 Haredim left Jerusalem and 42,000 left Bnei Brak ([Haredi Institute via Ynet, Dec 2024](https://www.ynetnews.com/jewish-world/article/h1cch618jg)).
Work divides the community by sex. Haredi women's employment has risen to about the level of other Jewish women; Haredi men's has been flat for a decade.
<Chart id="haredim.employment" />

Haredi men earn on average 49% of what other Jewish men earn ([IDI via The Media Line, Dec 2025](https://themedialine.org/headlines/israel-democracy-institute-report-finds-stalled-integration-of-ultra-orthodox-men-as-community-growth-accelerates/)).

Poverty and home ownership have to be read together, and the sources disagree on both. IDI counts 33% of Haredi families below the poverty line in 2023, against 14% of other Jewish families, and IDI's report, as summarized by The Media Line, says 75% of Haredim own their apartments ([IDI, Dec 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30207/final-final-haredi-shnaton-2025-pdf.pdf); [The Media Line, Dec 2025](https://themedialine.org/headlines/israel-democracy-institute-report-finds-stalled-integration-of-ultra-orthodox-men-as-community-growth-accelerates/)). The Haredi Institute counts 40% of Haredi households as poor in 2022, against 11% of other Jewish households, and puts Haredi home ownership at about 65%, down from 69%, against 61% among other Jews ([Haredi Institute, 2025](https://machon.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/english-digital-1-1-1.pdf)).
How their towns have voted, 2019–2022

The table combines five towns: Bnei Brak, Modi'in Illit, Beitar Illit and Elad, each more than 94% Haredi in the Haredi Institute's 2023 count, and Kiryat Ye'arim. It shows how these towns voted, computed from the Central Elections Committee's locality files; it is not a count of how every Haredi voted.
<Chart id="haredim.towns" />

About nine in ten votes in these towns go to UTJ or Shas in every election. Likud took between 2.6% and 5.1%. The only outside list that grew was the Religious Zionism joint list, which the Israel Democracy Institute places [on the far right](https://en.idi.org.il/israeli-elections-and-parties/parties/otzma-yehudit/): after Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit joined it in 2021, it took 5.7% and then 5.4%, with 11.2% in Elad in 2022. Turnout in the five towns ran from 76.3% to 80.0%, against 67.4% to 71.5% nationally.
The split between the two Haredi parties differs from town to town. Elad is the one town where Shas leads:
<Chart id="haredim.cities2022" />

Surveys show the same picture. In IDI's pooled post-election surveys, self-identified Haredim voted 58% UTJ, 28% Shas, 7% Religious Zionism–Otzma and 4% Likud in 2022; 86% voted for a Haredi list, down from 89% in 2021 ([IDI, June 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64807)). Nationally, Shas won 8.25% and 11 seats in 2022 and UTJ 5.88% and 7 seats ([CEC, Nov 2022](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)).

Shas's vote reaches well beyond Haredim. A veteran Shas activist told the Times of Israel in August 2026: "Shas has a base of four seats. It will hold on to that no matter what. But everything beyond that is up for grabs." The paper describes the rest as moderately traditional, working-class voters on Shas's periphery ([Times of Israel, Aug 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/eisenkot-threatens-to-siphon-traditional-voters-away-from-a-panicking-shas/)).

For 2026, UTJ filed one list, but with three factions, for the first time apart from a few days in 1992: Degel HaTorah, Agudat Yisrael and a new faction, Homat Torat Yisrael, led by Meir Porush and Elyakim Stark, whose members may split from UTJ once elected ([Davar, Sept 2026](https://www.davar1.co.il/696518/)). Asked in July 2026 to commit to Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc after the election, UTJ's Moshe Gafni cited his rabbi's ruling that "as of now, there is no bloc," and Agudat Yisrael answered, "First you pass the laws, then we'll talk," according to a Channel 12 report cited by the Times of Israel ([Times of Israel, July 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-said-seeking-haredi-loyalty-after-election-but-party-leaders-noncommittal/)). Only 36% of Haredim said they would vote for the same party as always, against 7% of the public ([IDI, Aug 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65364)). No 2026 survey of Haredi vote intention with a full Haredi sample was found.
What they think on the issues

**The draft.** Draft orders and arrests of yeshiva students who did not report (called "draft evaders" in Israeli debate) are covered on the [Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft) page. In early 2024, IDI found that Haredim were "the only group in which the majority of respondents think that the new circumstances created by the war should not affect the issue of conscription of Haredim in the future" ([IDI, March 2024](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/53305)). In July 2026, IDI found "very high levels of support among Haredim" for the law to halt arrests of what it called "deserters," against 25.3% support among Jews overall ([IDI Voice Index, July 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65483); [IDI data, July 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/media/31733/july-2026-index-data.pdf)). In 2025, 0.3% of Haredi men aged 21 to 44 served in the reserves in an average month, against 1.7% of secular men ([IDI, Aug 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65427)).

**Courts.** Haredi trust in the Supreme Court fell from 11% in 2023 to 7% in 2024 and 3% in 2025, and 93.5% agreed that the court "intervenes too much in government decisions" ([IDI Democracy Index, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).
<Chart id="haredim.trust" />

**War and hostages.** Haredi trust in the IDF was 61% in 2025, below every other Jewish group. Yet the share agreeing that "Israel ensures the security of its citizens" rose from 23% in 2022 to 68% in 2025, while among secular Jews it fell from 52% to 30% ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). In August 2025, a majority of Shas and UTJ voters supported "the release of all the hostages in exchange for the cessation of hostilities and the withdrawal of the IDF from all of the Gaza Strip," while support for Jewish settlement in Gaza was highest among Haredim ([IDI, Sept 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61601)). In September 2026, about a quarter of Haredim said October 7 was central to their vote, against about three-quarters or more of secular Jews ([IDI, Sept 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)).

**West Bank.** No 2026 survey publishes a Haredi figure on the West Bank. Pew's 2025 report combines Haredim with Datiim: 78% of that group said continued settlement building helps Israel's security (secular Jews 27%), and 9% think Israel and a Palestinian state can coexist peacefully (secular 25%) ([Pew, June 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/06/pg_2025.06.03_israel_report.pdf)).

**Religion and state.** 41% of Haredim name parties' positions on religion and state as the most influential factor in their choice, against 17% of non-Haredim; 5% name security ([IDI, Aug 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65364)). In 2025, 73% said the democratic component of the state is too dominant relative to the Jewish one ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

**Economy.** 3% of Haredim name the economy as their most influential factor, against 21% of non-Haredim ([IDI, Aug 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65364)). Haredim are the Jewish group most satisfied with their own lives: 85% call their personal situation good or very good, against 43% of secular Jews ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).
Who they are

On June 1, 2026, after six yeshiva students were arrested (by the group's own count), the Jerusalem Faction, a movement of about 60,000, used its "national alert system" to block Route 4 at the Ganot Interchange, the entrance to Jerusalem, and roads in Bnei Brak, Safed and Netivot.

Masorti Israel
Who Israel's traditional (masorti) Jews are, how they overlap with Mizrahi Israel, how the development towns have voted since 2019, and where they stand on the issues.
Size, growth and geography

Traditional Jews, *masortim* in Hebrew, sit between secular and religious on the scale Israeli surveys use to ask Jews how they see themselves. The Central Bureau of Statistics splits them in two: "traditional, not so religious" and "traditional-religious." Together they are the second-largest Jewish group after the secular: 35.8% of Jews aged 20 and over in the Central Bureau of Statistics' newest count (21.8% plus 14.0%) ([CBS via VIN News, September 2026](https://vinnews.com/2026/09/09/israel-enters-5787-with-population-growth-high-birthrate-and-rising-emigration/); [Ynet](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/sjc9lpcufl)).

The same CBS series gave 33.5% a year earlier ([CBS via Jerusalem Post, September 2025](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-868315)), a large one-year jump for which no published explanation was found. The Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 sample gives 31.9% (13.0% traditional religious, 18.9% traditional non-religious), weighted to CBS figures ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Pew's 2014–15 survey found 29% ([Pew, 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). Asked for a main identity, 19% choose "masorti," and about 45% use it as a secondary one ([JPPI, 2023](https://jppi.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/traditionalism_heb_2023-WEB-1.pdf)).

No fertility or growth figure for traditional Jews as a group was found. Nor could a CBS table of religiosity by town, or the CBS socio-economic ranking of each town, be obtained, so this page describes geography through places whose population history is known.

The best known are the development towns: "around 30 development towns created in the 1950s and 1960s mainly in the north and south of Israel, primarily to house immigrants from North Africa" ([Times of Israel, April 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/why-the-left-keeps-failing-in-the-pro-likud-periphery-home-to-25-of-israelis/)). This page follows six of them: Sderot, Netivot and Ofakim near Gaza; Dimona in the Negev; Beit She'an and Kiryat Shmona in the north. The wider periphery, the development towns plus Ashdod, Ashkelon and Beersheba, held just under a quarter of Israel's Jews in 2019 (same source).
Masorti and Mizrahi

"Masorti" and "Mizrahi" (Jews whose families came from the Middle East and North Africa) are often used as if they meant the same thing. They overlap but are not the same. Most Mizrahim are not masorti: in Pew's survey, "a plurality of Sephardim/Mizrahim (42%) identify as Masortim," about three in ten as secular, and most of the rest as religious or Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) ([Pew, fieldwork 2014–15](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/identity/)). And some traditional Jews are Ashkenazi or from the former Soviet Union.

Mizrahi is now mostly a matter of self-description. In 2025, 35.2% of Jewish adults called themselves Mizrahi, 39.8% Ashkenazi and 15.3% mixed ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Self-described Mizrahim placed themselves 73% on the right, 20% in the center and 5% on the left; Ashkenazim 49%, 31% and 18.5% (same source). Yet the old ethnic divide rarely registers as such: asked which tension in Israeli society is sharpest, about 2% of Jews chose Mizrahim versus Ashkenazim and 55% chose right versus left (same source).
How their towns have voted, 2019–2022

These tables show places, not people. They are computed from the Central Elections Committee's locality result files ([CEC](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)), and each list appears under the name it ran under that year.
<Chart id="masorti.six-towns" />

Three things stand out. Likud ran above its national share in every one of these towns in every election, but its peak was March 2020 (50.7% across the six) and it fell back to 40.2% in 2022. The 2022 change was a shift within the right, not away from it: the Religious Zionism joint list, carrying Itamar Ben-Gvir's [Otzma Yehudit](/parties/otzma), rose from under 1% for Otzma alone in 2020 to 17.0% in the six towns and 24.6% in Sderot, against 10.8% nationally. And the four lists that went on to form the 2022 government (Likud, Shas, United Torah Judaism and Religious Zionism) took 84% of the six towns' vote, against 48% nationally (CEC, computed).
<Chart id="masorti.towns-2022" />

[Shas](/parties/shas), a Haredi-led party with a traditional base, is covered as a party on the [Haredim page](/communities/haredim). Here it matters for its traditional voters: its share in the six towns rose from 15.7% to 22.2% between April 2019 and 2022. Netivot, where it took 42.5%, and Ofakim have large Haredi populations, so those results are not a traditional vote.

Surveys of people show the same rise for Religious Zionism. Pooled IDI surveys from November 2022 to October 2023 found that traditional voters chose Likud 46.5%, Religious Zionism 14%, Yesh Atid 13% and National Unity 12.5%; Likud was up from 39% in 2021 and Religious Zionism from 4% ([IDI, Finkelstein, June 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64807)). 57% of Likud's 2022 voters were traditional. The town and survey figures move differently (Likud fell in the six towns but rose among traditional voters nationally), and one should not be read as the other.

No published 2026 poll breaking vote intention down by religiosity was found. Palestinian citizens of Israel
About a fifth of Israel's population: who is counted, how their towns have voted since 2019, what they say on the issues, and why crime leads their agenda.

Palestinian citizens of Israel are the Arab Muslims, among them the Negev Bedouin, and Arab Christians who hold Israeli citizenship. Israeli officials, the Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) and Israeli pollsters such as IDI call them "Arabs," "Arab citizens" or "Arab Israelis." The name itself is contested, and the contest shows up in the surveys: asked in 2019 to pick a label, most picked a Palestinian one; asked to pick the single most important part of who they are, most pick "Arab" or "Israeli citizenship". This page uses "Palestinian citizens of Israel" and gives each source's own term where it quotes one.

CBS counts Druze inside its "Arab" population group, where they were 7.4% at the end of 2022 ([CBS, April 2023](https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/Society_&_Culture/druze-stats2023.pdf)). IDI and the Konrad Adenauer Program at Tel Aviv University write "Arab citizens" or "Arab society." The Abraham Initiatives uses "Arab citizens" in its crime report and "Palestinian citizens" on [its homepage](https://abrahaminitiatives.org/). Druze have [their own page](/communities/druze). Where a source breaks out Muslims and Christians, this page uses those figures. Where it does not, the figure includes Druze, and the page says so.
Size, growth and geography

How many there are depends on who is counted. CBS put Israel's Arab population at 2,173,000 in September 2026, 21.7% of the population by its count, which leaves foreign nationals out of the base; the total including them was 10,305,000 ([CBS via Times of Israel, September 9, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ahead-of-rosh-hashanah-israel-population-is-at-10305000-up-1-2-over-last-year/)). IDI notes that CBS's Arab count includes Arab residents of East Jerusalem, most of whom hold permanent residency rather than citizenship, and it includes Druze. IDI's split is for the end of 2020: 1,957,270 Arabs including East Jerusalem (21.1%), and 1,595,300 citizens without it (17.2%). The difference was "almost 362,000" East Jerusalem residents ([IDI, March 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/38540)). East Jerusalem Palestinians are outside this page's group and appear here only in that population note.

Among citizens outside East Jerusalem at the end of 2020, 82.9% were Muslim, 9.2% Druze and 7.9% Christian. Just over half (51.6%) lived in the north and Galilee, 19.7% in the Triangle, 17.5% in the Negev and 8.3% in mixed cities ([IDI, 2020 data](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/38540)). CBS counted 1.849 million Muslims in Israel in May 2026 ([CBS via TPS, May 26, 2026](https://tps.co.il/articles/israels-muslim-population-reaches-1-85-million-ahead-of-eid-al-adha/)).

The Negev Bedouin numbered about 325,000 at the end of 2023, about a fifth of the Negev's population. They grew sixfold between 1995 and 2023, and 48.6% are under 17. Between 70,000 and 90,000 live in what the State Comptroller calls "dispersed communities" and are commonly called unrecognized villages ([State Comptroller via Jerusalem Post, April 28, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-894474)). In the unrecognized villages, IDI found "only 10 elementary schools, and not a single secondary school" ([IDI, 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/38540)).

The newest income figures found are from 2018: 45.3% of Arab families were below the poverty line, against 13.4% of Jewish families, and Arab men earned 77% of what Jewish men earned ([IDI, 2018 data](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/38540)).
How their towns have voted, 2019–2022

Turnout was highest, 64.8%, in March 2020, when four parties ran as one Joint List, and fell to what IDI called "an all-time low" of 44.6% a year later, after Ra'am left ([IDI, April 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/34420)).

In 2022, Balad's 138,617 votes (2.91%) fell below the 3.25% threshold and won no seats, while Ra'am and Hadash–Ta'al won five each ([CEC results, computed](https://data.gov.il/dataset/votes-knesset)). In Arab and Druze localities that year, Ra'am took 35.2%, Hadash–Ta'al 28.8%, Balad 21.7% and the parties IDI classes as Zionist 14.3% ([IDI, December 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47986)).

For 2026 two lists ran: Ra'am under Mansour Abbas, and a re-formed Joint List of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad. The Central Elections Committee disqualified both in September. On October 2 the Supreme Court unanimously reinstated them, and Balad's leader Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy after the court told him a majority of the nine justices favored disqualifying him ([Al Jazeera, October 2, 2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2/israels-supreme-court-overturns-election-panel-ban-on-arab-parties)). In three TV polls after the lists were filed, the Joint List polled at 7–8 seats and Ra'am at 4–6 ([Times of Israel, September 10, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/election-polls-show-little-change-continued-deadlock-after-party-slates-finalized/)). In May, KAP projected Arab turnout of 53% if the parties ran as three separate lists, as in 2022 ([KAP, May 2026](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)). Pollster Yousef Makladeh estimated that a Hadash–Ta'al–Balad slate could lift it "from about 53% to 59%" ([Ynet, August 2, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/s1xafktsfg)).
What they think on the issues

The best cross-tabulation is IDI's Democracy Index 2025: 364 Arab respondents interviewed by phone in Arabic in May 2025, including Druze ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). The newest Arab-sector survey used here is KAP's, from April 26 to May 3, 2026. Its sample of 500 also includes Druze. Neither survey was taken after the October 2 ruling.

**What decides the vote.** Asked which issue would most affect their choice of party, 49.1% of Arab respondents named the cost of living, against 16.8% of Jews ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Crime is the top item on the community's agenda: 71.3% named it the most important issue in May 2026 ([KAP](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)). The Abraham Initiatives' count of those killed more than doubled from 2022 to 2023 and has stayed near that level ([Abraham Initiatives, December 2025](https://abrahaminitiatives.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2025-Crime-and-Violence-Report.pdf)).
<Chart id="palestinian-citizens.killed" />

**[The Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft).** Only 1.7% named Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription as their deciding issue, against 16.6% of Jews ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Palestinian citizens are not drafted: it has been "the declared policy of the Israeli army" not to draft Arabs, IDI's Mordechai Kremnitzer and Talya Steiner wrote ([IDI, June 2013](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/6807)). The question asked of them is civic service. In May 2026, 75.8% supported voluntary non-security civic service for Arab high-school graduates ([KAP](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)).

**[Courts](/issues/courts).** The Supreme Court is the institution Arab respondents trust most (40%), yet 55.5% also say it "intervenes too much in decisions made by the government." The judicial overhaul was the deciding issue for 11.2% ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

**[War and hostages](/issues/war-hostages).** In late 2023, 56% agreed with Mansour Abbas's statement that the October 7 attack did "not reflect Arab society, the Palestinian people, and the Islamic nation," and 33% disagreed ([IDI, December 2023](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/52016)). Trust in the IDF in 2025 was 28% among Muslims and 34% among Christians ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). In November 2025, 74.6% said the war had damaged Arab-Jewish relations ([KAP](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18732)).

**[West Bank](/issues/west-bank).** Asked for the most realistic solution, 46.4% chose two states on the 1967 lines, 21.4% said there is no solution and 18.7% chose one state (May 2026). In May 2023 only 17.2% chose two states, and 55.6% said there was no solution ([KAP](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)). The question asks what is realistic, not what is preferred. See also [a Palestinian state and the 2026 vote](/issues/palestinian-state).

**[Religion and state](/issues/religion-state).** 80% of Arab respondents say the Jewish component of Israel's identity is too dominant, against 44% of Jews ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). The 2018 Nation-State Law, passed 62–55 ([Reuters/AP via ABC News, July 19, 2018](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-07-19/israel-passes-controversial-jewish-nation-state-law/10014970)), declares: "The realization of the right to national self-determination in the State of Israel is exclusive to the Jewish People." It gives Arabic "a special status," where Arabic had been an official language before ([Knesset English text](https://main.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/Documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawNationState.pdf)).

**[Economy](/issues/economy).** Beyond the cost of living, 73.4% called their own economic situation fairly good in November 2025, the highest share KAP had recorded in the past year ([KAP](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18732)).

**Joining a government.** 77.2% support an Arab party joining the next coalition: 43.3% any coalition, 33.9% only a center-left one ([KAP, May 2026](https://dayan.org/file-download/download/public/18837)). In IDI's survey, 86% of Arab respondents back Arab parties in government, against 27% of Jews ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Both figures include Druze.

Religious Zionists
Who Israel's national-religious Jews are, how their towns have voted since 2019, what they think on the six election issues, and why the 2026 vote split them.
Size, growth and geography

Religious Zionists, also called national-religious Jews (*dati leumi* in Hebrew), combine Orthodox practice with full participation in the Zionist state: army service, state schools of their own, and a political movement that has been at the center of West Bank settlement. In the Central Bureau of Statistics' 2026 survey, 12.4% of Jewish adults described themselves as "religious" (*dati*), the official category closest to this group ([CBS via Ynet, Sept 2026](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/sjc9lpcufl)). That is about one Jewish adult in eight.

Surveys that ask about the group by name give similar figures. The Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 Democracy Index found 12.9% of its Jewish sample identifying as "national religious / Haredi leumi", a category that includes the stricter Hardal camp ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Pew's 2014–15 survey put Datiim at 13% of Israeli Jews ([Pew, 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). Among men aged 21 to 44 the share is higher, 14.7%, because the group is young ([IDI, Jan 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/57912)).

The growth shows up among children. State-religious schools took 29,470 of the 138,406 Jewish first-graders who started school in 2025–26, or 21.3%, up from 19.6% in 2000 ([Education Ministry figures via Times of Israel, Aug 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/for-the-1st-time-religious-1st-graders-in-israel-outnumber-secular-ones-by-thousands/)). Those schools also enroll children from traditional families, so enrollment is not the same as family identity. CBS fertility figures cited by the Jewish People Policy Institute give women who call themselves *dati* 3.88 children on average, against 2.0 for secular women; the page does not state the data years ([JPPI, 2023](https://jppi.org.il/en/%D7%94%D7%A2%D7%A8%D7%9B%D7%94-%D7%A9%D7%A0%D7%AA%D7%99%D7%AA-2023/s/5.4/)).

No CBS table of the national-religious population by town or district could be obtained for this page. The best evidence of where the movement is concentrated is the vote: in West Bank settlements such as Beit El, Eli and Kedumim, its lists take most of the ballots (see below and [Settlers](/communities/settlers)).

The Hardal camp (from *Haredi leumi*, "Haredi-national") is the movement's strictest wing. IDI offers it as a separate answer in its surveys and describes it as "a relatively small group" ([IDI, June 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64807)); the CBS has no Hardal category, and no primary source gives its size. The Open University sociologist Yagil Levy calls it "the ideological core of the settlement movement," controlling "a dense network of hesder yeshivas and religious pre-military academies," and "a Hardal minority, comprising only a few percentage points of the Jewish population" ([K. La Revue, Feb 2026](https://k-larevue.com/en/2026/02/05/on-the-evolution-of-the-idf-interview-with-yagil-levy/)).

The group carries a large share of the reserve burden. In 2025, 4.3% of men aged 21 to 44 who define themselves as religious served in the reserves in an average month, against 1.7% of secular men and 0.3% of Haredi men, by CBS Labor Force Survey data ([IDI, Aug 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65427)). National-religious men were 14.7% of men 21–44 but 27.4% of male reservists in 2024 ([IDI, Jan 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/57912)). The full reserve chart is on the [Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft) page. In officer ranks, Orthodox men rose from 2.5% of infantry officer-course graduates in the early 1990s to more than 25%, by figures in a 2015 report that cites a 2013 book edited by Reuven Gal, a former IDF psychologist ([CS Monitor, Apr 2015](https://www.csmonitor.com/World/Middle-East/2015/0417/In-Israel-s-army-more-officers-are-now-religious.-What-that-means)). No official dataset of officers since then, or of fallen soldiers by religiosity, has been published.
How their towns have voted, 2019–2022

The table shows how these towns voted in the five elections from April 2019 to November 2022, computed from the Central Elections Committee's locality files. Five are West Bank settlements; Givat Shmuel is inside the Green Line. A town is not a population group: these towns have residents who are not national-religious, and soldiers' envelope ballots are counted nationally, not by town, which matters for a group that serves heavily.
<Chart id="religious-zionists.towns" />

Three patterns stand out. In Beit El, Eli and Kedumim, the vote consolidated behind the Religious Zionism list once Naftali Bennett's Yamina faded: Beit El went from 71.1% for the Union of Right-Wing Parties in April 2019 to 83.2% for Religious Zionism in 2022. Kiryat Arba gave Otzma Yehudit 23.2% when it ran alone in September 2019, and Likud is strong there in every cycle (21–45%). Efrat is the other end of the range: New Right and then Yamina led there in every election to 2021, and in 2022 Ayelet Shaked's Jewish Home still took 15.4% and National Unity 6.9%, against 1.19% and 9.08% nationally.

A survey view points the same way. In IDI's pooled post-election surveys, national-religious voters (Hardal included) gave the Religious Zionism joint list 45% in 2022, up from 30% in 2021, as Yamina's 27% gave way to Jewish Home's 9%; Likud held at about 23% and 22.5%, and lists of the opposition took 9% and 10.5% ([IDI, June 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64807)). The joint list was not mainly this group's party, though: only 43% of its 2022 voters were national-religious, and 37% were traditional (see [Masorti Israel](/communities/masorti) for Otzma Yehudit's base).

For 2026 the movement's lists ran apart. Religious Zionism ran with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut, Otzma Yehudit ran alone, and Ofer Winter's new Amcha Yisrael ([People of Israel](/parties/poi)) competed for the same voters. A Dialog poll of national-religious voters for Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, taken Aug 31–Sept 2, 2026 among 508 members of Dialog's online panel (484 of them asked again after the Religious Zionism–Zehut union; margin of error 4.4 points), is the only 2026 survey of the group found:

**The Haredi draft.** In the Dialog poll, this was the issue on which the fewest respondents felt the government represented their views: 32% said it represented them to a large or very large extent on Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) enlistment and equal sharing of the burden, against 68% on settlement and 61% on security policy, while 37% said it represented them little or not at all. 15% named the draft as their most important issue ([Ynet, Sept 2026](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/elections2026/article/sydameiozg)). In March 2026, asked about the government's decision to suspend the Military Service Exemption Law and transfer billions of shekels to Haredi institutions, 37% of national-religious respondents called it "a political deal that prioritizes sectoral interests" and 34% "a responsible decision" ([IDI, March 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63856)).

**Courts.** Trust in the Supreme Court stood at 19% among national-religious Jews in 2025, against 66% among secular Jews, and 75% agreed that the court "intervenes too much in government decisions" ([IDI Democracy Index, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

The share agreeing that "Israel ensures the security of its citizens" rose from 32% in 2022 to 65% in 2025, while among secular Jews it fell from 52% to 30% ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). Russian-speaking Israelis
Who the immigrants from the former Soviet Union and their children are, how their towns have voted since 2019, and what little is known of their views.
Size, growth and geography

How many Russian-speaking Israelis there are depends on who is counted. About 1.25 million people came from the Soviet Union and its successor states between 1989 and mid-2023, about 13% of Israel's population and about 17% of its Jews ([Ze'ev Khanin, Riddle, August 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)). Khanin puts the share of them who later left Israel again at about 14%. A December 2025 Jerusalem Post report put the number of eligible voters who immigrated from the former Soviet Union at "around one million" ([JPost, December 2025](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-879843)).

Fewer people choose the label when asked. Asked their ethnicity in the Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 Democracy Index, 5.3% of Jewish respondents chose "FSU immigrant" ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

**Who is Jewish.** Immigration runs under the Law of Return, which admits the grandchildren of Jews; the Chief Rabbinate counts only those Jewish under halacha. More than 300,000 of the 1989–2019 arrivals were registered as non-Jews ([Khanin, 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)); a 2019 estimate put about 400,000 people in Israel, most from the former Soviet Union, as not recognized as Jewish by the Rabbinate ([Times of Israel, January 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/why-most-new-immigrants-to-israel-arent-considered-jewish/)). With no civil marriage in Israel, they cannot marry in a state-sanctioned wedding. Their share of each year's arrivals has risen steeply.
<Chart id="russian-speakers.not-recognized" />

**The 2022–25 arrivals.** After Russia invaded Ukraine, more than 47,000 people came from Russia and 15,500 from Ukraine between February 2022 and June 2023; those from Russia alone were almost two-thirds of all new citizens in that period ([Khanin, 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)). Arrivals from Russia fell from 19,535 in 2024 to 8,553 in 2025 ([Jewish Virtual Library, September 2026](https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/latest-population-statistics-for-Israel)). Many are thinking of leaving: in an April 2025 survey of immigrants from the former Soviet Union who arrived from 2014 to 2025, about 60% said they were considering moving to another country, 77% of those aged 18–34, against about a quarter of all Jews ([IDI, fieldwork April 2025, published December 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/62287)).

**Where and how old.** The Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) locality tables could not be reached for this page, so no town-by-town share of immigrants is given here. One CBS figure touches on age: people born in the former USSR are 35.8% of the Holocaust survivors living in Israel ([CBS, May 2024](https://www.cbs.gov.il/he/mediarelease/doclib/2024/132/11_24_132e.pdf)).
How their towns have voted

Election results are reported by place, not by origin, so the tables below show six whole towns where Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu has run well above its national share. Khanin describes it as a party whose voters, like Liberman himself, came from the former Soviet Union ([Khanin, 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)). They show how these towns voted, not how Russian speakers voted.
<Chart id="russian-speakers.yb-towns" />

Three things stand out. [Yisrael Beiteinu](/parties/yb) peaked in all six towns in September 2019, the election in which it won eight seats; by March 2020 Liberman was refusing to join a coalition with Shas and United Torah Judaism, the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) allies of Likud ([France 24, March 2020](https://www.france24.com/en/20200301-israel-s-netanyahu-tries-to-poach-russian-vote-from-old-rival)). It has fallen in every one of these towns at each election since. And by 2022 it was below its April 2019 level in five of the six towns (Haifa is the exception, 8.1% against 7.3%), while its national share was higher than in April 2019: 4.5% against 4.0% ([CEC, computed](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)).
<Chart id="russian-speakers.likud-towns" />

Likud did not pick up what Yisrael Beiteinu lost. Its share in these towns peaked in 2020 and in 2022 was below its April 2019 level in all six. In Nof HaGalil, Arab parties took 25.6% of the 2022 vote ([CEC, computed](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). Turnout in several of these towns was far below the national figure.
<Chart id="russian-speakers.turnout-2022" />
Estimates of the group's own vote, list by list, exist only to April 2019; for 2022 there is only a bloc estimate.

For 2022, Khanin estimated that the Netanyahu bloc took "no more than one-third" of the Russian-speaking vote ([Khanin, 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)). In a poll of 663 immigrants from the former Soviet Union published in December 2025, 23% chose Yisrael Beiteinu and 17% Naftali Bennett, and 69% said they did not want Benjamin Netanyahu to continue as prime minister ([Lazar Research, for a study led by former Yisrael Beiteinu MK Elina Bardach-Yalov at the Jerusalem Multidisciplinary College, via JPost, December 2025](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-879843)). Nationally, Yisrael Beiteinu stood at 6 to 10 seats in late-August 2026 polls ([Wikipedia polling table, to August 31, 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2026_Israeli_legislative_election)). What they think on the issues

No survey published in 2026 breaks out Russian speakers on any of the issues, and the major surveys (IDI, INSS, INES) publish no breakdown by Soviet origin after 2022. The one recent source is the Lazar poll above (published December 2025; fieldwork date and question wording not published), the only poll of this group found.
