On the draft of Haredi yeshiva students, see [the Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft).
- **Courts.** No group data.
- **War and hostages.** No group data on the war or the hostages. 56% said they were concerned about personal and national security (Lazar).
- **West Bank.** No group survey. Khanin describes the community as still belonging to the right-wing camp and backing Israel's Jewish identity in its ethno-national sense ([Khanin, 2023](https://ridl.io/war-aliyah-of-russian-speaking-jews-to-israel-past-experience-and-new-surprises/)).
- **Religion and state.** No survey of this group on civil marriage was found. The related fact is the one above: hundreds of thousands of citizens not recognized as Jewish by the Rabbinate cannot marry in a state-sanctioned wedding in Israel. The only older data point: 55% of first-generation immigrants from the former Soviet Union said they believe in God, against 70% of the second generation ([Pew, fieldwork 2014–15, the only source](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). See [religion and state](/issues/religion-state).
- **Economy.** 68% named the cost of living as their main concern, 74% were dissatisfied with the government's monetary policy and 72% with the country's direction (Lazar).

Secular Israel
Who Israel's secular Jews (hilonim) are, where they live, how their towns have voted since 2019, and where they stand on the issues of the 2026 election.
Size, growth and geography

Secular Jews, *hilonim* in Hebrew, are often called "Ashkenazi" or "Tel Aviv" Israel. Both words are shorthand, not a description. The first comes from the overlap with Jews of European origin: Pew found that "fully two-thirds of Ashkenazim identify as secular (Hiloni) Jews, compared with about three-in-ten of Sephardim/Mizrahim" ([Pew, fieldwork 2014–15, published 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/identity/)). But the overlap is partial, and origin itself is blurring: in 2025, 15.3% of Jewish adults described their origin as mixed ([IDI, Democracy Index 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). "Tel Aviv" names the group's best-known city, which is not all of it: the secular also live in the Sharon suburbs, Haifa and the kibbutzim, and Tel Aviv-Yafo itself includes Jaffa and many traditional and religious voters.

By the Central Bureau of Statistics' count, 39.6% of Jews aged 20 and over call themselves secular, the largest single group but not a majority ([CBS via Ynet, September 2026](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/sjc9lpcufl); age range per [VIN News](https://vinnews.com/2026/09/09/israel-enters-5787-with-population-growth-high-birthrate-and-rising-emigration/)). The rest: 21.8% traditional, not so religious; 14.0% traditional-religious; 12.4% religious; 11.5% Haredi (ultra-Orthodox).

The same CBS series gave 42.7% a year earlier ([CBS via Jerusalem Post, September 2025](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-868315)); no published explanation for the one-year drop was found. The Israel Democracy Institute's 2025 sample, weighted to CBS figures, puts secular Jews at 43.6% of Jewish adults ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)).

Growth is slow. In 2022 secular women had about two children each, against about six and a half for Haredi women; these figures are read from a Taub Center chart of CBS-based estimates. Taub projects that secular women reaching their early forties in the mid- to late 2030s will have had "around 1.6 children" ([Taub Center, December 2025](https://www.taubcenter.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Demography-2025-ENG-7.pdf)). Emigration (see below) is the other half of the story.

No CBS table of religiosity by city could be obtained, so the geography rests on where the secular vote shows up: Tel Aviv-Yafo, Givatayim, Ramat HaSharon, Herzliya, Hod HaSharon and the kibbutzim. The 241 kibbutzim of the Kibbutz Movement had 173,911 residents in 2022, under 2% of the population ([CBS localities file, 2022](https://www.cbs.gov.il/he/publications/doclib/2019/ishuvim/bycode2022.xlsx)). The secular are the most educated Jewish group in the newest comparison available, which is more than ten years old: 45% of Hiloni adults held a college degree, against 23% of Masortim and 13% of Haredim ([Pew, fieldwork 2014–15](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/education-values-and-science/)).
How their towns have voted, 2019–2022

The tables below show places, not people. They are computed from the Central Elections Committee's locality result files ([CEC](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)), and each list appears under the name it ran under that year.
<Chart id="secular.largest-list" />

The pattern across five elections has three phases. In 2019–20 these places gave Blue and White, the joint list of Benny Gantz and Yair Lapid, between 43% and 60% of their vote. By March 2021 that list had split, and the vote scattered across Yesh Atid, Labor, Meretz, Blue and White and New Hope; Labor led in the kibbutzim. In 2022 it re-formed behind Yesh Atid, which took 33–42% in the five cities.
<Chart id="secular.vote-2022" />

The secular right is real but small in these places. Likud took 15–22% in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Givatayim and Ramat HaSharon in every one of the five elections, 21–27% in Herzliya, and under 9% on the kibbutzim. In 2022 the four lists that went on to form the government (Likud, Shas, United Torah Judaism and the Religious Zionism joint list) took 26.7% in Tel Aviv-Yafo, 21.7% in Givatayim and 11.0% on the kibbutzim, against 48.4% nationally (CEC, computed). Meretz fell below the threshold nationally in 2022 while taking 10.9% in Tel Aviv-Yafo and 13.9% on the kibbutzim.

Surveys of people, not places, tell the same story. Pooled IDI surveys from November 2022 to October 2023 found that secular voters chose Yesh Atid 39%, Likud 20%, Labor and Meretz 16% and National Unity 13%, and that 74% voted for opposition parties ([IDI, Finkelstein, June 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64807)). 78.5% of Yesh Atid's Jewish voters were secular, and so were 32% of Likud's.
No published 2026 poll breaking vote intention down by religiosity was found. The parties that competed for these voters in 2026 are on the [party pages](/parties).
What they think on the issues

Politically the secular are not one camp: 23.8% place themselves on the left, 37.7% in the center and 37.2% on the right ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). On some issues they are close to united anyway.

**The Haredi draft.** This is the nearest thing to consensus. 71% chose drafting all young Haredi men except a small number of outstanding yeshiva students; 4% wanted to leave things as they are ([IDI, September 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61845)). See [the Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft).
<Chart id="secular.draft" />

**Courts.** One of the widest gaps between groups is over the Supreme Court: 66% of secular Jews trust it, against 3% of Haredim ([IDI, May 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). 72.5% of secular Jews say decisions opposed to basic democratic values are not democratic even if a Knesset majority passes them. Their trust in the government is 9% and in the Knesset 8%. See [courts and the judicial overhaul](/issues/courts).
<Chart id="secular.trust-court" />

**War and hostages.** IDI reports these questions by political camp, not religiosity. In September 2025, 94% on the left, 80% in the center and 48% on the right said the hostages should be the main goal of the war ([IDI, September 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61845)). No survey giving the secular figure itself was found. See [the war and the hostages](/issues/war-hostages).

**West Bank.** 66.5% of secular Jews said security forces treat violent settlers "too leniently," against 20.5% of national-religious Jews ([IDI, December 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/62468)). 21% supported Jewish settlement in the Gaza Strip in both November 2024 and August 2025 ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61601)). See [the West Bank](/issues/west-bank).

**Religion and state.** Secular is not the same as non-observant: 47% of secular Jews fast on Yom Kippur, fully or partly, and 20% attend a service ([IDI, July–August 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66240)). 23% name religious–secular as the sharpest tension in Israeli society ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). See [religion and state](/issues/religion-state).

**Economy.** No survey of secular economic attitudes was found. The mood is the darkest of any group: 9% call Israel's overall situation good, against 42% of Haredim, and 38.5% are optimistic about the country's future ([IDI, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). See [the economy](/issues/economy).

Settlers
Who the roughly 540,000 Israelis in West Bank settlements are, where they live, and why they vote as three different blocs rather than one.

"Settlers" is a cross-cutting group: it is defined by where people live, not by religion or origin. It takes in Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) families in large towns a few kilometers over the Green Line, commuters in suburban towns near Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, and national-religious communities deep in the occupied West Bank. The usual shorthand, 36% Haredi, 36% religious Zionist and 28% secular, is the settler leadership's own estimate, from the Yesha Council in May 2023. Newer counts confirm only the Haredi third.
Size, growth and geography

On January 1, 2026, 541,085 Jews lived in West Bank settlements, not counting East Jerusalem ([Interior Ministry population registry, compiled by former National Union MK Yaakov Katz for Bet El Institutions, which he founded, January 2026](https://jr.co.il/ys/West_Bank_Jewish_Population_Stats_Jan_2026.pdf)). That is 5.32% of Israel's population ([JNS, February 2026](https://www.jns.org/exclusive-judea-samaria-jewish-population-grew-at-twice-israels-overall-rate-in-2025/)). Counting the Jewish neighborhoods of East Jerusalem as well, the total is "over 750,000" in 147 settlements ([EU, 2025 settlements report](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/2025%20Report%20on%20Israeli%20settlements%20in%20the%20occupied%20West%20Bank.pdf)). Israel does not treat those neighborhoods as settlements; the EU, the UN and Peace Now do.
<Chart id="settlers.count" />

The settler population grew 2.2% in 2025, double Israel's 1.1% ([registry compilation, January 2026](https://jr.co.il/ys/West_Bank_Jewish_Population_Stats_Jan_2026.pdf)). The growth is not where an American reader might expect. Ma'ale Adumim, the best-known suburban settlement, has stopped growing: 40,943 residents in February 2021, 40,800 in January 2026. Over the same five years the Modi'in Illit bloc grew 13.8%, Beitar Illit 15.7%, Samaria 21.5%, the Jordan Valley 25.8% and Eastern Etzion 35.0% (same source). The growth is in the Haredi cities and in small communities far from the Green Line.
**Who they are.** Three estimates agree that about a third of settlers are Haredi. They disagree on the rest, partly because they measure different things.
<Chart id="settlers.composition" />

**Where they live.** The two largest settlements, Modi'in Illit and Beitar Illit, are Haredi cities in the West Bank. They are counted in settler totals here, but they are covered mainly on [the Haredim page](/communities/haredim). Beitar Illit's mayor said in 2017, "We came here due to the housing distress" ([Times of Israel, 2017](https://www.timesofisrael.com/black-is-the-new-orange-30-of-settlers-are-now-haredim/)). Next come suburban settlements (in Israeli usage, "quality-of-life" settlements) such as Ma'ale Adumim, Givat Ze'ev and Ariel. By this site's classification, 26.7% of settlers live in them ([registry compilation, January 2026](https://jr.co.il/ys/West_Bank_Jewish_Population_Stats_Jan_2026.pdf)). The remainder live mostly in about 80 other communities, most of them small and national-religious, plus the older farming villages of the Jordan Valley.
<Chart id="settlers.towns" />

**Outposts.** Peace Now, an Israeli group that opposes settlement, counted 86 new outposts in 2025 ([Peace Now, February 2026](https://peacenow.org.il/en/summary-of-2025-in-settlements)), against a previous record of 26 in 2023 ([EU, 2025 report](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/2025%20Report%20on%20Israeli%20settlements%20in%20the%20occupied%20West%20Bank.pdf)). By the same EU report's count, using Peace Now and Kerem Navot figures, farm outposts "effectively control more than 1,070,000 dunams — approximately 18% of the West Bank." The government approved 104 new or retroactively legalized settlements over its four-year term ([Times of Israel, September 28, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/two-new-west-bank-settlements-inaugurated-with-cabinet-ministers-on-hand/)).

Forming a government
What happens between election night and a sworn-in government: the president's mandate, the legal deadlines, the confidence vote, and what 2019–2022 showed.
What a government needs

Israelis do not vote for a prime minister. They vote for a party list, and the 120 seats are shared out in proportion to the vote (see [how seats are counted](/how-it-works/seats)). The government is then built inside the Knesset. Under Basic Law: The Government, "the Government holds office by virtue of the confidence of the Knesset," and the prime minister must be a Knesset member ([Basic Law: The Government, Knesset translation, amended through Aug 2023](https://main.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/Documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawTheGovernment.pdf)).

No single party has ever won a majority of the seats, so every Israeli government has been a coalition, with between three and nine parties in the coalitions formed after elections ([IDI, Ofer Kenig, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63976)).

A new government takes office only when the Knesset votes to express confidence in it. The prime minister-designate presents the ministers, how their portfolios are divided and the government's policy guidelines, and "the Government shall be formed once the Knesset has expressed confidence in it" (art. 13). The law does not demand an absolute majority: a government can be approved if more members vote for it than against it. In practice, IDI notes, governments formed after elections "have almost always enjoyed the confidence of a majority of Knesset members (at least 61 MKs)" ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63976)). That is why 61 is the number that coalition arithmetic is built around, including in the [Coalition Builder](/coalition-builder).

A coalition also has to keep that support. The Knesset dissolves automatically if it does not pass a state budget by the end of March, or within 145 days of a new government taking office ([IDI, Assaf Shapira, Jan 28, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63274)).
The clock

The process starts when the Central Elections Committee publishes the official results. The president then consults the representatives of every list entering the Knesset and, within seven days of the official results, gives "the task of forming a government" to one Knesset member who agrees to take it on (art. 7). This is the step usually called getting "the mandate."

The law gives the president no rule for choosing. IDI's explainer says the president "typically" picks the leader of the largest party, "but this is by no means mandatory"; the deciding factor is who seems to have the best prospect of winning the Knesset's confidence ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63982)).
<Chart id="forming-a-government.clock" />

Put end to end, the time limits in articles 7 to 10 come to at most 117 days after the official results are published (a total computed from the law's own limits). If they all run out, the Knesset is treated as having dissolved itself, and the election falls on the last Tuesday before 90 days have passed (art. 11). IDI's summary: the law allows three attempts, and "in almost all cases, the leader who was given the first chance to form a government succeeded in doing so" ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63976)).
How long it takes

From election day to a sworn-in government has taken between 20 and 100 days in Israel. In the past two decades no government has been sworn in less than 50 days after an election ([IDI, Kenig, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63982)). The record is from 1955, when 100 days passed. In the state's first two decades the process had no time limit ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63976)).
Majorities have often been thin. The chart shows how many Knesset members belonged to each coalition when it was formed, as IDI counts them.

2019–2022: five elections in under four years
The four-year cycle broke down in 2019, and the clock was tested at almost every step.

After the April 9, 2019 election, Benjamin Netanyahu failed to form a coalition in the 42 days allowed. The deal fell apart over the bill on drafting Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva students: Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu insisted the bill pass unchanged, and the Haredi parties refused. The Knesset then voted 74–45 to dissolve itself and set a new election for September 17 ([Times of Israel, May 30, 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-for-new-elections-on-september-17-after-pm-fails-to-form-coalition/)). It was the first Israeli election that failed to produce a government ([Times of Israel, Dec 12, 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-calls-another-election-for-march-the-third-in-a-year/)).

After September, every stage of the law was used. Netanyahu tried first and gave up. On October 23, 2019, President Reuven Rivlin gave the task to Benny Gantz of Blue and White, who had 28 days ([Times of Israel, Oct 23, 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/charged-with-forming-coalition-gantz-asks-netanyahu-to-join-vows-to-heal-rifts/)). Gantz failed too. Over the next 21 days no Knesset member gathered the 61 signatures needed for a third attempt, so the Knesset dissolved at midnight on December 11 and set an election for March 2, 2020 ([Times of Israel, Dec 12, 2019](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-calls-another-election-for-march-the-third-in-a-year/)).

In March 2020 Rivlin gave the first mandate to Gantz, not Netanyahu ([Jerusalem Post, Mar 16, 2020](https://www.jpost.com/Breaking-News/Gantz-arrives-at-Presidents-House-to-receive-mandate-to-form-govt-621147)). The two men then formed a rotation government, which was sworn in on May 17, 2020 by 73 votes to 46 ([Times of Israel, May 17, 2020](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/new-government-officially-sworn-in-with-parliamentary-vote/)). It never passed a 2020 budget, and the Knesset dissolved in December 2020. This is the only time an election has been brought forward because a budget failed ([IDI, Jan 28, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63274)).
After March 2021 Rivlin again gave Netanyahu the first chance, saying:
Reuven Rivlin. President of Israel. Al Jazeera. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/4/6/israels-president-to-announce-candidate-to-form-new-government. April 6, 2021
No candidate has a realistic chance of forming a government that will have the confidence of the Knesset.

Misreadings

**"The party with the most seats wins."** Winning the most seats brings no right to govern. After the 2009 election, President Shimon Peres gave the mandate to Netanyahu, whose Likud had 27 seats, instead of Tzipi Livni, whose Kadima had 28 ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63976)). What counts is who can win the Knesset's confidence, and that is a question of blocs. The [Coalition Builder](/coalition-builder) lets a reader try out the combinations.

**"Israelis elect the prime minister directly."** Israel did this only for a short period. A separate ballot for prime minister was first used in 1996, when Netanyahu beat Shimon Peres on May 29 ([IDI, June 17, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64732)). In IDI's words, direct elections were "quickly shelved in 2001, just five years after they were first introduced" ([IDI, Apr 20, 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/34340)). Since then the prime minister has been whichever Knesset member can put a government together.

**"Sixty-one is a legal requirement."** The confidence vote needs more votes for the government than against it, not 61. The Bennett government took office with 60 ([Times of Israel, June 13, 2021](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/bennett-lapid-government-wins-knesset-majority-netanyahu-is-out-after-12-years/)). Sixty-one is an absolute majority and a practical benchmark, not a stability guarantee. It can request a candidate in the final formation stage (art. 10), or install an alternative government through constructive no-confidence (art. 28) ([Basic Law: The Government](https://main.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/Documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawTheGovernment.pdf)).

**"A coalition deal settles who governs until the next election."** A coalition agreement sets out each partner's commitments and the posts it gets ([IDI, Apr 15, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63982)), but it lasts only as long as the Knesset majority behind it. On the day the 2020 unity government was sworn in, Netanyahu promised to hand the premiership to Gantz on November 17, 2021 ([Times of Israel, May 17, 2020](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-may-17-2020/)). The handover never happened: the Knesset dissolved in December 2020 over the budget ([IDI, Jan 28, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63274)).

**"Election night settles it."** Election night only starts the clock. Of the five elections from 2019 to 2022, two produced no government at all. For the three that did, the swearing-in came 58 to 82 days after the vote (counted from the dates in the table above).
From votes to seats
How Israel turns national votes into 120 Knesset seats: closed party lists, the 3.25% threshold, the Bader-Ofer count and surplus-vote agreements.
One country, one ballot, 120 seats

The Knesset has 120 members, and they are elected in "a single, nationwide constituency." Voters "elect party lists, not members of Knesset," and seats are shared out in proportion to the vote ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750)).

There are no districts. A voter in Haifa and a voter in Eilat choose from the same lists, and every valid vote goes into one national pool. Each list files a ranked slate of candidates before the election, and voters cannot reorder it. "If a party wins 10 seats, the first 10 people on the list become Knesset members" ([Center for Israel Education, Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)). For an American reader, the nearest picture is one at-large race for all 120 seats, in which people vote for a party's slate rather than for a person.

Thirty-eight lists qualified for the October 27, 2026 ballot ([Center for Israel Education, Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)). Each appears on the ballot under a short code of Hebrew letters; the [results page](/results) maps them to the parties.
The 3.25% threshold

A list needs at least 3.25% of the valid votes to win any seats at all; this has been the rule "since the 2015 election" ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750)). The threshold has been raised several times. Summaries of that history sometimes give different years for the last step; the two IDI accounts agree once the law is separated from the election: Ofer Kenig writes that the Knesset passed the 3.25% law in March 2014 ([IDI, Jan 26, 2015](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/5225)), and Assaf Shapira dates it to 2015, the first election held under it ([IDI, Nov 8, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46256)).
<Chart id="seats.threshold-history" />

How many votes 3.25% means depends on turnout, so the exact number is known only after the count. In 2022 it was 154,855 votes, 3.25% of 4,764,742 valid votes ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750); [Central Elections Committee, Nov 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). For 2026, with about 7.56 million eligible voters, the Center for Israel Education estimated before the vote that a list "will need 172,000 votes" ([Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)).

Votes for a list that falls short are not passed on to anyone. They drop out of the count before any seat is assigned ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750)). In 2022, lists under the threshold drew 417,400 votes in all ([Central Elections Committee, Nov 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). IDI put the wasted share at about 8.7%, an all-time high ([IDI, Nov 8, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46256)). Meretz won 150,793 votes (3.16%) and missed by 4,062. Balad won 138,617 (2.91%), and Jewish Home won 56,775 (1.19%) ([Central Elections Committee, Nov 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). Shapira notes that the two blocs' vote totals were "almost identical," but the Netanyahu camp won "a clear majority of 64 seats" ([IDI, Nov 8, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46256)).

How the seats are counted

The method is called Bader-Ofer, after Knesset members Yohanan Bader and Avraham Ofer. It dates from the Bader-Ofer Law, introduced in 1973, which was meant in part "to strengthen the larger parties" ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)). In effect it is the D'Hondt method, worked out in two stages ([Fruits and Votes, Sept 8, 2026](https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/09/08/israels-bader-ofer-method-of-allocating-seats-step-by-step/)). The steps below use the 2022 numbers. The arithmetic here is recomputed from the Central Elections Committee's totals and matches IDI's published figures ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750)).

1. **Count the valid votes** and remove those cast for lists under the threshold. In 2022, 4,347,342 votes remained.
2. **Set the price of a seat.** Divide the remaining votes by 120. In 2022 one seat cost 36,227 votes.
3. **Hand out whole seats.** Each list gets one seat for every full 36,227 votes. In 2022 this gave out 113 seats and left 7.
4. **Hand out the leftover seats one at a time.** Divide each list's votes by the seats it already holds plus one. The highest result wins the next seat. Then that list's figure is recalculated, and the process repeats. In this step, two lists with a surplus agreement count as one list.
5. **Split a pair's extra seats** between its two partners by the same rule.
<Chart id="seats.quotas-2022" />
<Chart id="seats.leftover-2022" />

Inside the Likud–Religious Zionism pair, Likud's figure (1,115,336 ÷ 31 = 35,978.58) beat its partner's (516,470 ÷ 15 = 34,431.33), so Likud took the first extra seat. Its new figure, 34,854.25, still beat Religious Zionism's, so Likud took the second as well and finished with 32 seats. Inside the other pairs, Shas took the Shas–UTJ seat, and National Unity and Yesh Atid took one seat each ([Central Elections Committee, Nov 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults); [Fruits and Votes, Sept 8, 2026](https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/09/08/israels-bader-ofer-method-of-allocating-seats-step-by-step/)).

Under the largest-remainder rule used for the Second through Seventh Knessets, the seven leftover seats would have gone to the seven largest unused remainders. That would have given seats to Labor and United Torah Judaism instead of Likud's second extra seat and Yesh Atid's (computed from the [Central Elections Committee's totals](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). The tilt toward size comes almost entirely at this stage. IDI's Shapira and Gideon Rahat write that apart from leftover seats, "there is almost no electoral advantage to large lists" ([IDI, April 27, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64020)).
Surplus-vote agreements

Before an election, two lists may sign a surplus-vote (or vote-sharing) agreement. When leftover seats are handed out, the pair "are treated as a single list": their votes are added together and divided by their combined seats plus one ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)). A pair is a bigger list, and the method favors bigger lists, so its chance of an extra seat goes up. Only two lists can sign an agreement together ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)).

The larger partner usually gets the extra seat, but not always. In 2021 the smaller partner won it in three pairs: Meretz over Labor, New Hope over Yamina, and Yisrael Beiteinu over Yesh Atid ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)).

An agreement counts only if both lists pass the threshold. If one fails, its partner "is considered not to have signed an agreement at all" ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)). That happened to Labor in 2022. Its agreement with Meretz lapsed when Meretz fell short ([IDI, April 27, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64020)), so Labor competed for leftover seats alone and won none.

For 2026, press reports describe three agreements as signed: [Yashar!](/parties/yashar) with [The Democrats](/parties/dem), [B'Yachad](/parties/byachad) with [Yisrael Beiteinu](/parties/yb), and the [Joint List](/parties/jl) with [Ra'am](/parties/raam). The Jerusalem Post reported that [Shas](/parties/shas) and [United Torah Judaism](/parties/utj) were expected to sign one ([Sept 10, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-908296)). Israel Policy Forum reported that [Likud](/parties/likud) and [Religious Zionism–Zehut](/parties/rz) planned to sign ([120 Project, Sept 10 entry](https://israelpolicyforum.org/onetwenty/)); a week after the two parties agreed on a deal, Channel 14 reported that it had not yet been signed ([Channel 14, Sept 15, 2026](https://www.c14.co.il/article/1702522)). Agreements can be filed until October 16 ([AIJAC, Sept 14, 2026](https://aijac.org.au/australia-israel-review/a-game-of-margins/)). Provisional [results estimates](/results) assume only those three press-reported signed pairs; the two unconfirmed pairs are excluded. Official filing has not been established.

Misreadings

**"A vote for a small party is a vote for its candidates in the voter's own district."** There are no districts. Every vote goes into one national count, and a list's seats go to the names at the top of its ranked slate ([IDI, March 16, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750); [Center for Israel Education, Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)). Below 3.25%, that vote elects no one.

**"Votes for a list that misses the threshold go to its allies."** They are discarded. A surplus agreement does not rescue them, because it counts only when both partners pass ([IDI, Oct 30, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47485)). In 2022, Meretz's 150,793 votes did nothing for Labor.

**"The threshold is about seats."** It is a share of valid votes, not a number of seats. In 2022, a list at exactly 154,855 votes would still have been worth four whole seats at 36,227 votes each ([Central Elections Committee, Nov 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). So that year no list could pass the threshold and win only one, two or three seats. Labor, at 3.69%, won four. Meretz, at 3.16%, won none.

**"The biggest party forms the government."** What matters is an arrangement that can win initial confidence, not the largest list. Sixty-one is an absolute seat majority and a practical planning target. After the 2009 election, Netanyahu formed a government "even though Kadima won one more seat than Likud," and Naftali Bennett later formed one at the head of the small Yamina faction ([IDI, April 27, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64020)). The steps that follow election day are on [forming a government](/how-it-works/forming-a-government).

**"Seats track the vote exactly."** They come close, but not exactly. The threshold drops some votes. The leftover-seat stage slightly favors large lists and pairs, and in 2022 that gave Likud a 32nd seat ([Fruits and Votes, Sept 8, 2026](https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/09/08/israels-bader-ofer-method-of-allocating-seats-step-by-step/)).
How Israelis vote
Who can vote, how a paper ballot is cast, why nearly one vote in ten comes in a double envelope, and how election night turns into a final count.
Who can vote

Any Israeli citizen aged 18 or over who is on the voter roll can vote ([Ynet, Oct 31, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjxzpztvo)). In 2022 the roll held 6,788,804 eligible voters ([Central Elections Committee, 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). For the October 27, 2026 election an estimated 7.56 million were eligible, 11% more than in 2022, mostly people who have turned 18 and newly naturalized citizens ([IsraelEd, Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)). The committee had not published its own 2026 total in the sources checked for this page.

Citizenship, not residence, is the test. About 350,000 Palestinians in East Jerusalem hold permanent residency rather than citizenship; they may vote in Jerusalem's municipal elections but not for the Knesset ([Inter-Agency Task Force, updated Dec 2022](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf)). Palestinians in the rest of the West Bank and in Gaza hold no Israeli status (same source), and the committee's results files list no Palestinian localities there. Israeli citizens who live in West Bank settlements vote where they live: Ariel and Ma'ale Adumim, for example, appear as localities in the committee's 2022 results file like any town inside Israel ([CEC, 2022](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). The [vote map](/vote-map) draws them that way.

Israel has almost no absentee voting. Only diplomats and official emissaries abroad may vote outside the country ([IDI, Feb 18, 2020](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/29786)). The law's list covers government employees posted overseas, including military personnel, and emissaries of the Jewish Agency, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund and Keren Hayesod, with their spouses and children up to age 20. In 2022 about 4,500 voters were registered at 103 polling stations in 101 missions ([Ynet, Aug 29, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/sjljnsl00zg)). Every other Israeli abroad must be in Israel on election day to vote. For 2026, the missions voted from October 20 ([Jerusalem Post, July 13, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-902333)).
How a Knesset vote works
The walk-through below holds for any Knesset election: one slip, one envelope, one box, and a second envelope for a voter away from home.
<BallotLead />
Election day

Election day is a national holiday, with public transport running normally ([Jerusalem Post, July 13, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-902333)). Most polling stations are open from 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.; smaller communities, hospitals and prisons from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. A voter still in line at closing time may still vote (same source). Salaried employees are entitled to a paid day off by law, and those who work that day get higher pay ([Ynet, Sept 18, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/business/article/sjkupwyffg)).

Voting is on paper, not machines ([IsraelEd, Sept 28, 2026](https://israeled.org/38-party-lists-israels-2026-parliamentary-election/)). The voter shows photo identification, and the polling-station committee checks the name on the roll. The voter is handed an envelope, steps behind a screen, takes one paper slip for the chosen list, seals it in the envelope and drops the envelope in the ballot box. A slip with writing on it, a torn slip, or an envelope holding more than one slip is disqualified ([Ynet, Oct 31, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjxzpztvo)).

Each list is identified by one to four Hebrew letters, and the committee reports its count by those letters, not by party name: in 2022 the Likud column in the results file was headed מחל ([CEC, 2022](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). Letters can pass from one alliance to another between elections. The 2026 letters for the lists this site tracks are on the [results page](/results), under "The ballot letters". For what the votes turn into, see [how seats are allocated](/how-it-works/seats).
Double-envelope votes

A voter who casts a ballot anywhere other than the assigned polling station votes in a double envelope, officially an "outer envelope." Most are members of the security forces stationed away from home. The rest include hospital patients and staff, prisoners and detainees, diplomats abroad, residents of senior-care facilities, and voters with disabilities, who may use any accessible polling station ([IDI, Nov 2, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46196)). Police officers who vote away from their own station use them too. Before counting, the committee gathers the double envelopes and checks that no one voted twice ([Ynet, Oct 31, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjxzpztvo)). For 2026, the committee decided that soldiers deployed in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza may be identified by their military tags and a fellow soldier, and that this procedure applies to double envelopes, "which are counted at a later stage" ([Ynet, July 30, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/byscqcurml)).

The share rose at each election from April 2019 to 2022, from 5.54% to 9.63% of valid votes (computed from the [CEC files](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). IDI notes that more voters now use accessible polling stations, and that in 2020 and 2021 tens of thousands of double-envelope votes were cast by people in quarantine or hospital and by residents of senior citizens' homes ([IDI, Nov 2, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46196)).
<Chart id="voting.envelopes" />

These votes are why the count moves after election night. Double-envelope voters are younger and more often soldiers than the electorate as a whole. IDI found that Arab lists' share of these ballots is less than half of their share among regular voters, and that Haredi lists also do worse in them, so an Arab list hovering near the threshold after the regular count can fall below it once they are added ([IDI, Nov 2, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46196)). The 2022 file shows the pattern: Ra'am won 1.7% of the double-envelope votes against 4.3% of the votes counted by locality, while Religious Zionism–Otzma Yehudit won 15.5% against 10.4% (computed from the [CEC file](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)).
<Chart id="voting.envelopes-2022" />
Turnout
National turnout ranged from 67.44% to 71.52% across the five elections of 2019–2022; in 2022 it was 70.63% ([CEC, 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)).
<Chart id="voting.turnout" />

Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has been lower and has swung far more. The Israel Democracy Institute's Arik Rudnitzky measures it in Arab and Druze localities. It fell to 49.2% in April 2019, after the Joint List broke up, and rose to 59.2% in September 2019 when it re-formed ([IDI, Sept 23, 2019](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/28660)). It reached 64.8% in March 2020, the highest in two decades ([IDI, Mar 10, 2020](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/30961)), then dropped to 44.6% in 2021 ([IDI, Apr 27, 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/34420)), and recovered to 53.2% in 2022 ([IDI, Dec 25, 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47986)). Because the measure leaves out double-envelope votes and Arab voters in mixed cities, it is not directly comparable with the national figure. More on the community is on the [Palestinian citizens of Israel page](/communities/palestinian-citizens).
<Chart id="voting.turnout-arab" />
Election night

Polls close at 10:00 p.m. Israel time, and the three main television channels, Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13, broadcast exit polls at that moment ([Ynet, Nov 1, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/h1tyl0a4s)). Counting starts at the polling stations at 10:00 p.m.; the ballot boxes then go to regional election committees, and the results are entered into the Central Elections Committee's system, which shows them as they arrive ([Ynet, Oct 31, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjxzpztvo)). Votes cast at the missions abroad are counted on election day after 10:00 p.m. (same source).

In 2022 the count ran into the next day. By Wednesday afternoon over 80% of the votes had been counted, and many of those still out were double-envelope ballots ([JTA, Nov 2, 2022](https://www.jta.org/2022/11/02/israel/as-vote-is-tallied-netanyahu-appears-headed-for-more-sweeping-victory-than-expected)). The committee's final 2022 locality file is dated November 8, a week after the vote ([CEC file](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). For 2026, official confirmation of the results was scheduled for November 4, with appeals possible until November 18 ([Jerusalem Post, July 13, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-902333)).
For the October 27, 2026 election, the committee's count is on the [results page](/results), and the steps that follow it are on the [government page](/government).
Misreadings

**"Israelis abroad can vote by mail or at a consulate."** There is no mail vote, and the consulate polling stations are open only to officials posted abroad and named national-institution emissaries, with their families. An Israeli who lives in New York, or is on vacation there on election day, cannot vote at the consulate ([Ynet, Aug 29, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/sjljnsl00zg)).

**"The exit poll is the result."** Exit polls are estimates. In 2022 the early exit polls put Meretz at 5 seats ([Jerusalem Post, Nov 1, 2022](https://www.jpost.com/israel-elections/article-721230)). In the final count Meretz won 3.16% of the vote, below the 3.25% threshold, and no seats ([CEC, 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)).

**"Election-night numbers are final."** About one valid vote in ten in 2022 was a double-envelope vote counted after the regular ballots, and those votes split differently from the rest. With 87.6% counted, Meretz stood at 3.19% and Balad at 3.02% ([Jerusalem Post, Nov 2, 2022](https://www.jpost.com/israel-elections/article-721318)); both finished lower, at 3.16% and 2.91% ([CEC, 2022](https://votes25.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults)). A list near the threshold is not in or out until the envelopes are counted.

**"Low turnout means apathy, the same everywhere."** National turnout has stayed near 70%, while turnout in Arab and Druze localities has swung by 20 points between elections, with the gap widest in 2021: 67.44% nationally, 44.6% in those localities ([CEC, 2021](https://votes24.bechirot.gov.il/nationalresults); [IDI, Apr 27, 2021](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/34420)).

**"Every Palestinian under Israeli control can vote."** Palestinian citizens of Israel can. Most East Jerusalem Palestinians are permanent residents, not citizens, and cannot vote for the Knesset, and Palestinians in the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, who hold no Israeli status, have no vote in it ([Inter-Agency Task Force, updated Dec 2022](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf)).
Who votes, and who doesn't
Citizenship, not residence, decides the Knesset vote. Who holds it, who does not, the Palestinian elections, and the legal findings about the gap.
Citizenship decides the vote

Israeli citizens aged 18+ listed in the voter register can vote for the Knesset ([Ynet, Oct 31, 2022](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjxzpztvo)), Palestinian citizens of Israel and Druze citizens on the same terms as Jewish citizens ([Inter-Agency Task Force, updated Dec 2022](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf)). Settlers who are citizens vote where they live ([CEC, 2022](https://media25.bechirot.gov.il/files/expc.csv)). Most Israelis abroad must come home to vote ([Times of Israel, Aug 15, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ballot-battlefield-takes-shape-as-sides-tussle-over-voters-homebound-and-homeward-bound/)); see [how Israelis vote](/how-it-works/voting).

**East Jerusalem.** Israel annexed East Jerusalem after 1967. The UN Security Council declared Israel's measures altering Jerusalem's status "null and void" and decided "not to recognize" the 1980 law proclaiming Jerusalem Israel's capital ([Resolution 478, Aug 20, 1980](https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=S/RES/478%281980%29&l=en&t=pdf)). Most of the city's 375,600 Arab residents (end of 2021, [Jerusalem Institute for Policy Research](https://jerusaleminstitute.org.il/en/publications/jerusalem-facts-and-trends-2023/)) hold permanent residency, not citizenship. They can vote in Jerusalem's municipal elections, though most do not, and cannot vote for the Knesset ([Inter-Agency Task Force](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf)). They may apply for citizenship ([Times of Israel, Jan 13, 2020](https://www.timesofisrael.com/unprecedented-1200-east-jerusalem-palestinians-got-israeli-citizenship-in-2019/)).

**The Golan Druze.** Israel offered citizenship to the Druze of the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights in 1981, and most long declined it. Since 2020, 6,779 have applied, 3,750 of them in 2025 ([Times of Israel, Mar 15, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/after-years-of-hesitation-more-druze-of-the-golan-heights-seek-israeli-citizenship/)). See the [Druze page](/communities/druze).

**The West Bank and Gaza.** Palestinians living there who are not Israeli citizens cannot vote for the Knesset; Palestinian elections operate separately ([Inter-Agency Task Force](https://www.acitaskforce.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Arab-Palestinian-Citizenship-and-Residency-2025.pdf); see below). The West Bank is occupied. Area C, more than 60% of it, is under full Israeli control ([Times of Israel/AFP, July 20, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/palestinian-builds-plane-shaped-guesthouse-in-west-banks-area-c/)). Outside East Jerusalem, West Bank Palestinians live under Israeli military rule beside settlers who have Israeli citizenship and the Knesset vote; the International Court of Justice found that "Palestinians in the West Bank are thus subject to military law and military courts, whereas settlers benefit from the criminal law and criminal justice system applicable to civilians in Israel" ([ICJ, July 19, 2024, para. 136](https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=A/78/968&l=en&t=pdf)). In all, about 5.4 million Palestinians, counting all ages, live in the West Bank, East Jerusalem included (3.3 million), and Gaza (2.1 million) ([OCHA, Dec 16, 2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/sites/default/files/OPT_Flash_Appeal_2026_EN_FINAL.pdf)); the Knesset vote depends on Israeli citizenship and voter registration. See the [West Bank page](/issues/west-bank).
Palestinian elections

The Palestinian Authority's last national elections were in 2005, when Mahmoud Abbas won the presidency, and 2006, when Hamas's list won 74 of 132 legislative seats ([Palestinian Central Elections Commission, 2005](https://www.elections.ps/Portals/0/pdf/SummaryPresidentialElectionsFinalResults2005.pdf); [2006](https://www.elections.ps/Portals/0/pdf/The%20final%20distribution%20of%20PLC%20seats.pdf)). Hamas took control of Gaza "in a violent coup against Fatah in 2007" ([Times of Israel, Apr 25, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/turnout-low-as-palestinians-in-west-bank-and-gaza-vote-in-local-elections/)).

Abbas called elections for May and July 2021 ([CEC, Jan 15, 2021](https://www.elections.ps/tabid/1127/language/en-US/Default.aspx)), then postponed them: "we decided to postpone the date of holding legislative elections until the participation of Jerusalem and its people is guaranteed" ([Al Jazeera, Apr 30, 2021](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/4/30/palestinians-polls-hamas-plo)). Israel's Foreign Ministry called the elections "an internal Palestinian issue" ([Al Jazeera, Apr 30, 2021](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/4/30/palestinian-factions-reject-abbas-decision-to-delay-polls)). The Times of Israel gives two reasons for the cancellation: the lack of guarantees for voting in East Jerusalem, and "prospects of Hamas gains at the expense of Fatah" ([July 9, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/abbas-declares-first-palestinian-legislative-elections-since-2006-to-be-held-nov-28/)).

Local elections were held on April 25, 2026, including in Gaza's Deir al-Balah ([CEC, 2026](https://www.elections.ps/tabid/1297/language/en-US/Default.aspx)); Hamas boycotted them in the West Bank ([Times of Israel, Apr 27, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/pa-leader-abbass-loyalists-win-local-elections-including-in-gazas-deir-al-balah/)). On July 9, 2026, Abbas set legislative elections for November 28, 2026, which, "if they take place, would mark the first such vote in two decades." Candidates must accept the PLO's program, "which includes recognition of Israel and support for a two-state solution" ([Times of Israel, July 9, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/abbas-declares-first-palestinian-legislative-elections-since-2006-to-be-held-nov-28/)).
The legal findings about the gap

Three human rights organizations have concluded that Israel's rule over Palestinians amounts to apartheid. The Israeli group B'Tselem wrote in January 2021 that "a regime that uses laws, practices and organized violence to cement the supremacy of one group over another is an apartheid regime," and that Israel's rule from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean meets that bar ([B'Tselem, Jan 12, 2021](https://www.btselem.org/publications/fulltext/202101_this_is_apartheid)). Human Rights Watch found that "Israeli authorities are committing the crimes against humanity of apartheid and persecution" ([HRW, Apr 27, 2021](https://www.hrw.org/report/2021/04/27/threshold-crossed/israeli-authorities-and-crimes-apartheid-and-persecution)). Amnesty International's secretary general, Agnès Callamard, said Israel's "cruel policies of segregation, dispossession and exclusion across all territories under its control clearly amount to apartheid" ([Amnesty, Feb 1, 2022](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/02/israels-apartheid-against-palestinians-a-cruel-system-of-domination-and-a-crime-against-humanity/)).

In a July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that Israel's "continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory is unlawful" (11 votes to 4), that Israel must end it "as rapidly as possible," and that it is obliged "to cease immediately all new settlement activities, and to evacuate all settlers" (14 to 1). On Article 3 of the UN convention against racial discrimination, which covers "racial segregation and apartheid," the court found that Israel's measures "impose and serve to maintain a near-complete separation in the West Bank and East Jerusalem between the settler and Palestinian communities," a breach of the article. It did not say which of the two it was ([ICJ, July 19, 2024](https://www.icj-cij.org/case/186)). In their own statements, President Nawaf Salam wrote that Israel's policy is "tantamount to apartheid"; Judge Georg Nolte wrote that the opinion "cannot be understood as finding that the prohibition of apartheid has indeed been violated."

Israel rejects these findings: its Foreign Ministry called the HRW report a "propaganda pamphlet" ([NPR, Apr 27, 2021](https://www.npr.org/2021/04/27/990993903/israel-accused-of-apartheid-crimes-by-human-rights-watch)) and Netanyahu answered the court that "the Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land" and that "no false decision in The Hague will distort this historical truth" ([Times of Israel, July 19, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/responding-to-false-icj-ruling-pm-says-jewish-people-cant-be-occupiers-in-their-own-land/)).
The Gaza legal record

**ICJ.** In *South Africa v. Israel*, brought under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, the court ordered provisional measures on January 26, 2024, by votes of 15–2 and 16–1: that Israel "take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts within the scope of Article II" of the convention, and enable "urgently needed basic services and humanitarian assistance" ([ICJ](https://www.icj-cij.org/node/203447)). It added measures on March 28 and May 24, 2024 ([ICJ](https://www.icj-cij.org/case/192/press-releases)). These are interim orders "ahead of a final decision" ([UN News, Jan 26, 2024](https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/01/1145937)), not a ruling on the merits. The court's then-president, Joan Donoghue, later said it had found that Palestinians had a "plausible right" to the convention's protection, and had not ruled on whether South Africa's claim was plausible, though it saw a risk of irreparable harm to that right ([BBC, Apr 26, 2024](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-68906919)). Israel's March 2026 filing argued that the court lacks jurisdiction and should dismiss the case ([Times of Israel, Mar 21, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/germany-pulls-support-for-israel-in-icj-genocide-case-as-it-faces-own-accusations/)).

**ICC.** On November 21, 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, finding reasonable grounds that they bear responsibility for "the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare; and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts" ([ICC](https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/situation-state-palestine-icc-pre-trial-chamber-i-rejects-state-israels-challenges)). It also issued one for Mohammed Deif of Hamas, whose case was closed in February 2025 after his death ([ICC](https://www.icc-cpi.int/palestine)). Israel's jurisdiction challenge was sent back for a new ruling in April 2025, and in December 2025 the warrants remained in place ([ICC, Apr 24, 2025](https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/situation-state-palestine-appeals-chamber-reverses-pre-trial-chambers-decision-israels); [Times of Israel, Dec 15, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/icc-denies-israeli-bid-to-halt-gaza-probe-maintains-warrants-for-netanyahu-gallant/)). Netanyahu's office called the accusations "antisemitic" and rejected them "with disgust" (same source).

**Famine.** On August 22, 2025, an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis found that "more than half a million people in Gaza are trapped in famine" and projected famine to spread "from Gaza Governorate to Deir Al Balah and Khan Younis Governorates" ([WHO, Aug 22, 2025](https://www.who.int/news/item/22-08-2025-famine-confirmed-for-first-time-in-gaza)). Netanyahu's office called it "an outright lie" ([Times of Israel, Aug 23, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahus-office-calls-gaza-famine-declaration-a-modern-blood-libel/)). In December 2025 the IPC found famine conditions no longer prevailing, though food security "remain[s] critical"; Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said the report portrayed a "distorted, biased and unfounded picture" ([Times of Israel, Dec 19, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ipc-monitor-says-famine-conditions-over-but-gaza-food-security-still-critical-israel-rejects-findings/)).

**UN inquiry.** On September 16, 2025, the UN Commission of Inquiry concluded: "The Commission finds that Israel is responsible for the commission of genocide in Gaza." Israel's Foreign Ministry said the report came from "Hamas proxies" ([Times of Israel, Sept 16, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/un-panel-claims-genocide-underway-in-gaza-israel-blasts-members-as-hamas-proxies/)).
The tolls

**Israel.** In the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, attackers killed some 1,200 people and abducted 251 ([Times of Israel, Oct 1, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/widely-cited-times-of-israel-archive-of-oct-7-fallen-now-available-on-social-media/)). On October 4, 2026, the [Defense Ministry reported](https://www.mod.gov.il/כתבות-ומבזקים/חדשות-משרד-הביטחון/שלוש-שנים-למלחמת-התקומה) 1,318 security personnel added to its official fallen roll since October 7, 2023. [JNS's October 4 report](https://www.jns.org/news/israel-news/israel-marks-1-318-slain-security-personnel-since-oct-7) attributes 1,029 civilians killed in terrorist attacks over that period to the National Insurance Institute. Both counts include October 7.

**Gaza.** The Gaza Ministry of Health, which operates under the Hamas-run authorities, reports 73,922 Palestinians killed as of September 23, 2026, 1,402 of them since the October 2025 ceasefire. OCHA attributes the count to the ministry, noting that figures "yet-to-be verified by the UN are attributed to their source"; the ministry had fully identified 71,444 of the dead by December 31, 2025, among them 21,283 children ([OCHA, Sept 23, 2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/reported-impact-snapshot-gaza-strip-23-september-2026); [OCHA, Sept 25, 2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026)).

**West Bank.** From January 2025 to August 2026, OCHA recorded that Israeli forces killed 284 Palestinians in the West Bank, Israeli settlers killed 25, and forces or settlers killed 13 more; Palestinians killed 20 Israelis there, 8 of them members of Israeli forces, and Palestinians from the West Bank killed three Israelis inside Israel in 2025 ([OCHA, Sept 14, 2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/sites/default/files/West%20Bank_info-graphic_14_September_2026.pdf)). See the [war and hostages](/issues/war-hostages) and [West Bank](/issues/west-bank) pages.
Misreadings

**"Arabs can't vote in Israel."** Palestinian citizens of Israel can; Ra'am and the Joint List are on the 2026 ballot ([Al Jazeera, Oct 2, 2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2/israels-supreme-court-overturns-election-panel-ban-on-arab-parties)). Those without a Knesset vote are non-citizens: most East Jerusalem residents, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. See [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens).

**"West Bank Palestinians have no elections."** They have Palestinian Authority elections, but none for the presidency since 2005 or the legislature since 2006; a legislative vote is set for November 28, 2026 ([Times of Israel, July 9, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/abbas-declares-first-palestinian-legislative-elections-since-2006-to-be-held-nov-28/)).

**"The ICJ has decided South Africa's case."** It has not ruled on the merits. Its 2024 orders were interim measures, and the case is pending ([UN News, Jan 26, 2024](https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/01/1145937)).
Courts and the judicial overhaul
Why Israel's fight over its Supreme Court is about who checks a governing majority, what Israelis think of it, and where each list stands.
What is at stake

Israel has no single written constitution. In 1950 the Knesset chose to write separate "Basic Laws" instead ([Knesset](https://main.knesset.gov.il/en/activity/pages/basiclaws.aspx)), and many can be passed or changed by a simple majority. The Knesset is the only legislature, with no second chamber ([Knesset](https://main.knesset.gov.il/EN/About/Pages/BranchesOfGovernment.aspx)). "In Israel, the Supreme Court is the only restraint on the power of the political majority," the Israel Democracy Institute wrote in 2022 ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46387)). In 1995 the court held that the Basic Laws have constitutional status and that it may void ordinary laws that infringe them; Supreme Court President Aharon Barak wrote that "the constitutional revolution occurred in the Knesset in March 1992" ([ruling, Nov 9, 1995](https://versa.cardozo.yu.edu/opinions/united-mizrahi-bank-v-migdal-cooperative-village)).

In January 2023 Justice Minister Yariv Levin announced a judicial overhaul: bar courts from voiding decisions as "unreasonable"; give the government a majority on the committee that picks judges; curb judicial review; let 61 Knesset members re-enact a struck-down law; and stop legal advisers' positions from binding ministries ([Times of Israel, Jan 4, 2023](https://www.timesofisrael.com/justice-minister-unveils-plan-to-shackle-the-high-court-overhaul-israels-judiciary/)).

On March 23, 2023 a bare Knesset majority amended a Basic Law so that the court cannot order a prime minister to take a leave of absence; removal requires physical or mental incapacity and 75% of ministers or Knesset members ([JTA, Mar 23, 2023](https://www.jta.org/2023/03/23/israel/netanyahu-vows-more-active-role-in-israels-judiciary-fight-following-a-day-of-tense-protests)). On July 24, 2023 the Knesset abolished the reasonableness standard ([Globes](https://en.globes.co.il/en/article-knesset-enacts-law-to-abolish-reasonableness-standard-1001453127)). On January 1, 2024 a full 15-justice panel struck that law down 8–7, and 12 of the 15 held that the court may review Basic Laws in exceptional cases ([ruling](https://versa.cardozo.yu.edu/opinions/movement-quality-government-israel-v-knesset); [NPR](https://text.npr.org/1222400537)). On January 3 it ruled 6–5 that the incapacity law was "clearly a personal amendment" and delayed it to the next Knesset ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/high-court-delays-contentious-law-shielding-netanyahu-from-recusal/)).
Protests and the security services

In 2023 hundreds of thousands protested weekly, and more than 10,000 veterans pledged to boycott reserve duty ([JTA, July 24, 2023](https://www.jta.org/2023/07/24/israel/israel-passes-first-law-weakening-supreme-court-following-months-of-civil-strife)). After Netanyahu fired Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, who had urged a pause, a general strike backed by the Histadrut labor federation shut universities on March 27, and Netanyahu paused the bills that evening ([JTA, Mar 27, 2023](https://www.jta.org/2023/03/27/israel/there-must-not-be-a-civil-war-netanyahu-gives-in-to-calls-to-postpone-judiciary-reform-in-significant-victory-for-protesters); [JTA](https://www.jta.org/2023/03/27/israel/a-historic-day-in-israel-ends-with-a-political-compromise-and-big-questions-about-the-future)). On April 27 an estimated 200,000 supporters rallied in Jerusalem ([JTA](https://www.jta.org/2023/04/27/israel/we-will-not-give-up-on-judicial-changes-right-wing-protesters-at-israels-largest-pro-reform-rally-are-told)).

Otzma Yehudit MK Almog Cohen said a refusal leader's views "seriously harmed the cohesion and security of the country, and were a catalyst for the events of October 7" ([Times of Israel, Dec 2, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/katz-nixes-reserve-duty-of-protest-leader-who-urged-refusal-to-serve-over-judicial-overhaul/)). On October 7, the Times of Israel reported, the army had "an unprecedented 120% turnout rate for reservists" ([Times of Israel, July 19, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/katz-orders-democrats-party-candidate-ousted-from-idf-reserves-over-call-to-refuse-service/)).

On March 21, 2025 the cabinet fired Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who then announced his resignation. On May 21 the court ruled 2–1 that the firing was improper and made while Netanyahu had a conflict of interest, but issued no orders since the case was moot. Netanyahu called the ruling "disgraceful" ([Times of Israel, May 21, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/high-court-rules-shin-bet-heads-dismissal-unlawful-pm-had-conflict-of-interest/)).
The next bench

In March 2025 the Knesset passed, 67 votes in favor, a law that removes the Israel Bar Association's two seats from the selection committee and lets justices be appointed without the sitting justices' consent, from the next Knesset on ([Times of Israel, Mar 27, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-greatly-boosting-political-control-over-judicial-appointments/)). The Supreme Court, sitting as the High Court of Justice, heard petitions against it on June 21, 2026; the Times of Israel counted nine of the 11 justices as critical of parts of it ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/regime-change-high-court-tears-into-coalition-bid-to-control-judicial-appointments/)). No ruling had been found as of October 5. Four of 15 seats are vacant and six more justices turn 70, the retirement age, within three years ([JTA, Sept 18, 2026](https://www.jta.org/2026/09/18/israel/judicial-reform-2-0-how-netanyahus-plans-to-reshape-the-courts-could-affect-israels-democracy)), so the next government could fill about two-thirds of the bench.

Supporters argue that unelected judges overrule voters. Levin promised that judges would no longer "choose themselves in back rooms with no protocol" (Times of Israel, Jan 4, 2023). Religious Zionism wants narrower rules on who may petition the court ([Ynet, Sept 22, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/hkcjtk1cme)). Conservative critics, IDI scholars write, hold that value judgments "should be decided by democratically elected representatives and not unaccountable judges" ([IDI, Feb 2023](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/47916)). The Kohelet Policy Forum, "a non-partisan research and action institute" by its own description, argues that "governmental legal counsel must be subordinate to appointed Ministers" ([Kohelet, July 16, 2026](https://www.kohelet.org.il/en/article/legal-advisors-must-answer-to-elected-ministers/)).

Yariv Levin. Justice Minister (Likud), announcing the overhaul. Times of Israel. https://www.timesofisrael.com/justice-minister-unveils-plan-to-shackle-the-high-court-overhaul-israels-judiciary/. January 4, 2023

We go to the polls, vote, elect, and time after time, people we didn't elect choose for us. Many sectors of the public look to the judicial system and do not find their voices heard. That is not democracy.

Yariv Levin. Justice Minister (Likud), in recordings aired by Kan. JTA. https://www.jta.org/2026/09/18/israel/judicial-reform-2-0-how-netanyahus-plans-to-reshape-the-courts-could-affect-israels-democracy. August 2026

We'll wait for the next term, when two-thirds of the Supreme Court justices' seats become vacant. I told them (the Supreme Court justices): I won't need to carry out a reform. You'll simply go extinct.

The government voted on August 4, 2025 to fire Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/high-court-freezes-dismissal-of-attorney-general-after-government-votes-to-fire-her/)); on December 14 seven justices, conservatives included, unanimously annulled the firing ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/high-court-annuls-firing-of-attorney-general-cabinet-ministers-urge-defiance-of-ruling/)). A law passed July 15, 2026, 65–51, lets the government reject the attorney general's opinions and control the post's appointment and dismissal; prosecution, including whether to investigate senior elected officials, stays with the attorney general. It takes effect in January 2027 ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/coalition-passes-law-gutting-attorney-generals-powers-removing-key-check-on-government/)). A dropped June draft would have let a new prosecutor general "reconsider the existing indictments against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu" ([Jerusalem Post, June 2, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-898054)).
Netanyahu's trial

Netanyahu has been on trial since May 2020: for fraud and breach of trust in Case 1000 (gifts from benefactors) and Case 2000 (alleged talks for favorable newspaper coverage), and also bribery in Case 4000 (regulatory decisions alleged to have benefited Bezeq shareholder Shaul Elovitch in exchange for favorable Walla coverage). He denies wrongdoing. On June 29, 2026 the judges again urged prosecutors to drop the bribery charge ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/judges-again-call-on-prosecution-to-drop-bribery-charge-from-netanyahu-trial/)). Ending his testimony on June 24, he called the case "a political assassination"; defense witnesses remain ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-wraps-up-trial-testimony-after-98-hearings-across-18-months/)). Supporters echo "his contention that the charges amount to a political witch hunt" ([Times of Israel, June 30](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ministers-coalition-mks-push-pardon-for-pm-after-judges-urge-dropping-of-key-charge/)). Watchdog groups argued the overhaul could affect his trial ([Times of Israel, Jan 3, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/high-court-delays-contentious-law-shielding-netanyahu-from-recusal/)).

In November 2025 he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon, without admitting guilt. On April 26, 2026 Herzog set it aside and proposed plea talks ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/herzog-pushes-for-new-plea-deal-talks-says-he-wont-consider-netanyahu-pardon-request-yet/)); as of June 30 his lawyers had not responded (Times of Israel, June 30).
The court and the 2026 election

On September 23, 2026 the Central Elections Committee voted 18–5 to disqualify the Joint List and 18–5 to disqualify Ra'am, on petitions from Likud, Otzma Yehudit and others citing Basic Law: The Knesset's bar on supporting armed struggle against Israel. The attorney general saw grounds only against Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh, over an October 8, 2023 article calling the Hamas assault "an important historic event"; the Joint List accused backers of the bans of "deepening racism" ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/election-panel-votes-to-bar-balad-chief-abu-shehadeh-over-alleged-support-for-terror/)). The law also bars incitement to racism and denying Israel's existence as a Jewish and democratic state; bans need Supreme Court approval, and the committee is almost all party lawmakers. On October 2 nine justices unanimously reinstated both lists, and Abu Shehadeh withdrew after the court's president told him a majority would bar him ([Times of Israel, Oct 2, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/supreme-court-unanimously-overturns-election-panels-ban-on-arab-parties/)). See [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens).
What Israelis think

In each of three IDI surveys since 2023, more Israelis opposed the overhaul or its timing than backed it. In March 2026, 52% said it was not correct to advance it now and 32% said it was ([IDI, March 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30641/israeli-voice-index-march-2026-eng-data.pdf)). The wording changed between surveys, so the chart shows each separately.
<Chart id="courts.overhaul" />

It ranks low as a vote factor: 18% of Jewish respondents named the judicial system as a first or second factor, behind security (39%), the economy (38%), the draft (27%), religion and state (26%) and the party leader (23%) ([IDI, Sept 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)).

Jewish trust in the Supreme Court fell mostly before the overhaul: from 69% in 2003 to 41% in 2022, and 42% in May 2025 ([IDI Democracy Index 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/media/30427/the-israeli-democracy-index-2025-full-english-version.pdf)). The 2026 index is not out.
<Chart id="courts.trust" />

In May 2025, 83% of left-wing Jews trusted the court against 21.5% on the right, and 66% of secular Jews against 3% of Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) (same source). IDI's reading is that "political identity outweighs religiosity."
<Chart id="courts.trust-groups" />

In January 2025, 79% of Arab respondents opposed the overhaul, against 50.5% of Jews ([IDI, Jan 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/57945)). Yet in May 2025, 55.5% of them said the court "intervenes too much," against 50% of Jews (Democracy Index 2025). IDI's "Arabs" include Druze.
What the parties say

Coalition parties that answered Ynet's September 2026 survey want to curb the court; Likud declined to answer. Zehut, Moshe Feiglin's party, says the court "has accumulated powers that were never explicitly granted by legislation" ([Ynet, Sept 22, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/hkcjtk1cme)). Yashar!, B'Yachad and the Reservists want a Basic Law setting rules for legislation or judicial review; Yisrael Beiteinu wants a written constitution put to a referendum; Blue and White would limit the court's intervention in government decisions.
<Positions issue="courts" />
Misreadings

**It is not a fight over a culture-war docket.** Israel's fight is over the court's structure and power. Conservative justices joined the attorney-general ruling, and the conservative justice Alex Stein criticized the selection law at the June 2026 hearing ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/regime-change-high-court-tears-into-coalition-bid-to-control-judicial-appointments/)).

**"Judicial review" means something different.** The U.S. court reviews laws against a written constitution that is hard to amend. Israel's reviews them against Basic Laws, many passable by a simple majority, and since 2024 it says it may review those too.

**Appointments work differently.** Justices are not nominated and confirmed; they retire at 70. Under the old rules a Supreme Court appointment needed 7 of the committee's 9 votes, with three justices on it ([IDI, Dec 2022](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/46674)).
**The court also rules on who may run.** In 2026 it overturned the election committee's bans on the Joint List and Ra'am.

documents.title: Cost of living and the economy

blocks.text: Cost of living and the economy
High prices, a war bill of about NIS 350 billion, a contested budget, and who works and who serves: what the economy means in the 2026 election.
What is at stake

Prices in Israel are rising slowly, but they are high. Inflation was 1.9% year on year in May 2026 ([Moody's via Ynet, July 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/business/article/rkqzvq4vfe)), after 2.6% in 2025 ([Bank of Israel Annual Report 2025](https://www.boi.org.il/en/communication-and-publications/regular-publications/bank-of-israel-annual-report/bank-of-israel-annual-report-2025-1/)). But food and non-alcoholic drink cost 52% more than the average across 38 OECD countries, second only to South Korea, with dairy, eggs and meat each 64% above the average ([OECD data via Times of Israel, July 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/food-and-beverage-prices-in-israel-52-higher-than-oecd-average-report/)). That comparison is the most recent found, and it is more than two years old.

Housing is moving in two directions. Home prices fell 1.5% in the year to May–June 2026, and prices had declined in eight of the previous 12 months, according to Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) data ([CBS via Times of Israel, September 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/housing-snapshot-september-2026-prices-inch-upward-after-sharp-decline/)). Rents rose. In the CBS release for April–May 2026, rent for new tenants was up 6.6% on a year earlier and for renewing tenants 2.6% ([CBS via Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/business-and-innovation/banking-and-finance/article-902755)).

The war has also left a bill. The Bank of Israel puts war-related costs for 2023–2026 at about NIS 350 billion. Public debt rose from 60.5% of GDP in early 2023 to 68.5% at the end of 2025, and the 2025 deficit was 4.7% of GDP ([Jerusalem Post, October 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-910242)). Moody's cut Israel's rating by two notches to Baa1 in September 2024 and raised its outlook to stable in February 2026 ([Times of Israel, February 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/moodys-boosts-israels-credit-outlook-to-stable-as-ceasefires-in-gaza-lebanon-hold/)), then kept the rating unchanged in July ([Ynet, July 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/business/article/rkqzvq4vfe)). S&P affirmed an A rating with a stable outlook in May ([Ynet, May 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/business/article/sj3dyricze)). Fitch rates Israel A with a negative outlook. In March 2026 Fitch warned that rising public debt and prolonged military activity could derail growth and deficit reduction, and said Israel's "fractious domestic politics" could hinder fiscal consolidation ([Reuters via KELO, March 2026](https://kelo.com/2026/03/27/fitch-affirms-israels-a-rating-with-a-negative-outlook/)).
<Chart id="economy.war-bill" />

The 2026 budget passed the Knesset 62–55 on March 30, 2026, a day before the deadline that would have triggered automatic elections. Defense received NIS 143 billion. The government approved a 3% across-the-board cut to all ministries except Defense, and funding for Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) educational institutions rose from NIS 4.1 billion to NIS 5.17 billion. A late-night amendment adding NIS 800 million for Haredi programs passed 107–4; opposition members seemed to treat it as routine and backed it automatically ([Times of Israel, March 30, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-approves-2026-budget-israels-largest-ever-sending-billions-to-haredi-institutions/)). The fight over coalition money for sectoral institutions, which Israelis call "coalition funds", goes back further. On March 10 the cabinet approved more than NIS 5 billion of it, including NIS 1.56 billion for Torah institutions such as yeshivas and kollels; a study by the Berl Katznelson Center think tank found that NIS 2.2 billion went to the Haredi community ([Times of Israel, March 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/cabinet-okays-1-6-billion-in-coalition-funds-including-715-million-for-ultra-orthodox/)). Yesh Atid MK Vladimir Beliak put the total at a "record high" of NIS 6 billion ([Jerusalem Post, March 22, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-890836)). Neither source reconciles the two figures.

Under the budget sits a question about who works. Haredi men's employment rate was 52% in 2015 and 53% in 2025, against a government target of 65% by 2030 ([Labor Ministry report via Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/business-and-innovation/opinion/article-901982)). Researchers at the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) called it "a decade of stagnation" in the integration of Haredi men and noted that over the same period there has been "rapid growth in the number of yeshiva and kollel students," men in full-time Torah study ([IDI via The Media Line, December 2025](https://themedialine.org/headlines/israel-democracy-institute-report-finds-stalled-integration-of-ultra-orthodox-men-as-community-growth-accelerates/)).
<Chart id="economy.employment" />

The rates in the chart come from different sources and years. Haredi women work at a far higher rate than Haredi men. Arab men's employment was 77% in early 2025, slightly below its 2023 peak of 79%, and the Taub Center expects Arab women's rate to surpass Haredi men's ([Taub Center, June 2026](https://www.taubcenter.org.il/en/pr/pon-2026/)).
The governor of the Bank of Israel told the cabinet that funding for yeshiva students, "many of whom are not part of the workforce, and do not serve in the army," harms growth:
