Amir Yaron. Governor, Bank of Israel. Times of Israel. https://www.timesofisrael.com/bank-of-israel-governor-warns-funding-yeshiva-students-draft-exemptions-threatens-growth/. December 4, 2025
Such budgets harm long-term growth and living standards, and their impact will increase over time

Some people are also leaving Israel. In 2025, 69,300 residents left and 19,000 returned ([CBS via Ynet, December 2025](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/r1zatkmnzg)). A Tax Authority study of emigrants from 2015 to 2024 found that the number leaving from the high-tech sector grew by about 150% ([Jerusalem Post, August 2026](https://www.jpost.com/business-and-innovation/banking-and-finance/article-904992)). High-tech was 57% of Israeli exports in the first half of 2025 ([Israel Innovation Authority, September 2025](https://innovationisrael.org.il/en/press_release/innovation-report-2025/)). The Tax Authority estimates a potential tax loss of about NIS 700 million for each new cohort of emigrants.
What Israelis think

Among Jewish Israelis, the economy and security are close to even as reasons for a vote. In IDI's Israeli Voice Index, fielded August 31 to September 3, 2026, 38% of Jewish respondents named "economy and the high cost of living" as the first or second factor in their vote, and 39% named foreign affairs and security ([IDI, September 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)).

The economy matters more to some groups than to others. Among Jewish voters who place themselves in the Center, it ranks first, at 40.5%. On the Left, religion and state comes first (39%) and the economy second (34%). On the Right, security leads at 47%; IDI did not publish the Right's figure for the economy. Among Arab respondents the economy comes second (46%), after crime in Arab society (53.5%) ([IDI, September 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)). IDI published no breakdown of this question by religiosity, so there is no published figure for Haredim.
<Chart id="economy.economy-by-group" />

The survey also asked about the national mood. 61% of respondents called it poor. Among Jewish respondents that share fell from 73% a year earlier to 65.5%, and among Arab respondents from 58% to 40% ([IDI, September 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)).
What the parties say

Most lists have not published a full economic platform for 2026. The table below gives each party's own words where they could be found, a news outlet's summary of them where marked, or the wording of IDI's party guide where that is the only source.
<Positions issue="economy" />
Misreadings

**"It's the economy" does not work the same way.** An American reader may expect the economy to decide the vote. The IDI data show it at the top only for Center voters and Arab citizens. Many Israelis name prices as a worry and still decide their vote on security, the draft, or religion and state.

**Economic positions do not sort by bloc.** Within the Netanyahu bloc, the Likud charter, as IDI describes it, refers to "support for a competitive free market," while Shas threatened to withhold its budget vote until poor Haredi children received food-stamp support. Yisrael Beiteinu, in the opposition, is described by IDI as holding "right-wing fiscal positions" ([IDI party guide](https://en.idi.org.il/israeli-elections-and-parties/parties/yisrael-beitenu/)). In Israeli politics "right" and "left" are not, mainly, economic labels.

**The employment figure is tied to the draft.** "53% of Haredi men work" can read like a job-training problem. In Israel it is bound up with yeshiva funding and military service. The Finance Ministry's chief economist found that non-Haredi Jewish men are 36% of all employees but 83% of those absent from work for reserve duty ([Finance Ministry via Arutz Sheva, August 2026](https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/432226)). The same figures run through the debate over the [Haredi draft](/issues/haredi-draft). See also [religion and state](/issues/religion-state).

**"Cost of living" means price levels.** With inflation under 2%, the complaint is about prices that are already high. B'Yachad, in the opposition, promises to break up food cartels; it does not target the central bank.

**A strong market and strained households can both be true.** Tel Aviv's benchmark index rose 52% in 2025, and a third of households spend more than they earn ([Time, July 2026](https://time.com/article/2026/07/13/israel-war-economy-cost-ordinary-israelis/)).
The Haredi draft
Why yeshiva students' exemption from military service broke a government, what Israelis think should replace it, and where each party stands.
What is at stake

The conscription law makes every Israeli citizen who reaches 18 liable for service ([Zeidan Atashi, former Druze MK, via Jewish Virtual Library](https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/druze-in-israel-and-the-question-of-compulsory-military-service)). In practice the army calls up Jewish men and women and Druze men ([Pew Research Center, March 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/03/21/5-facts-about-israeli-druze-a-unique-religious-and-ethnic-group/)), and Circassians; Muslim, Bedouin and Christian Arab citizens are not called up and may volunteer ([Atashi, via Jewish Virtual Library](https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/druze-in-israel-and-the-question-of-compulsory-military-service)). Compulsory service "will remain at 32 months", the Knesset decided in July 2026, against the army's request for more ([Ynet, July 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/h1nremv4gl)). Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men have, for most of the state's history, been able to defer service year after year while studying full-time in yeshiva. David Ben-Gurion, the first defense minister, ordered the deferral for students for whom "Torah is their calling" (*Torato umanuto*). It was capped at about 400 a year until 1970; a quota of 800 was set in 1975, and "following the coalition agreement of 1977, the quota was abolished altogether," the Supreme Court recounted in 1998 ([Supreme Court, HCJ 3267/97, Dec 9, 1998, via Cardozo Law School](https://versa.cardozo.yu.edu/opinions/rubinstein-v-minister-defense)). Why Palestinian citizens of Israel are not drafted is a separate question, covered on [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens).

The Supreme Court struck down the laws that put the deferral into statute: the Tal Law in 2012, and a 2015 amendment in 2017 ([IDI, January 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63168)). On June 25, 2024, a unanimous nine-justice panel ruled there is "no legal basis for avoiding the recruitment of yeshiva students" and that the state may not fund the yeshivas of men who should be drafted ([Times of Israel, June 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/in-historic-ruling-high-court-says-government-must-begin-drafting-haredi-men-into-idf/)). In April 2026 it ordered personal sanctions, including loss of discounted housing and daycare subsidies ([IDI, April 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64062)). On September 3, 2026, it voided a July 2026 law shielding yeshiva students from arrest. The ruling counted about 73,664 "draft evaders", the term used in Israeli debate (this page says yeshiva students who did not report), of whom 219 had been arrested ([Jerusalem Post, September 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-907553)).

Since October 7, 2023, the argument has been about manpower as much as principle. The IDF says it is short about 12,000 soldiers, 6,000–7,500 of them in combat roles ([IDI, January 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63168)). Average reserve duty was 94 days in 2024 and 78 in 2025 ([Times of Israel, June 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/average-reserve-duty-in-2025-was-78-days-37-of-reservists-are-parents-biggest-number-comes-from-tel-aviv/)).

Haredi enlistment has roughly doubled, from about 1,800 a year before the war to at least 4,000 in 2025–26, a preliminary figure, against an army target of 4,800 and about 14,000 Haredi men reaching draft age each year ([Times of Israel, July 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/idf-chief-tells-haredi-commanders-army-must-grow-as-data-shows-uptick-in-enlistment/); [Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-904035)). Draft orders are a different measure: in the 2024 draft year, about 24,000 initial orders produced 798 enlistees ([IDI, January 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63168)).
<Chart id="haredi-draft.enlistment" />

The two sides argue in different terms. Supporters of drafting Haredim speak of an equal burden; the court wrote that "in the midst of a severe war, the burden of inequality is more acute than ever" ([Times of Israel, June 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/in-historic-ruling-high-court-says-government-must-begin-drafting-haredi-men-into-idf/)). Haredi leaders speak of Torah study as "the spiritual defense of the People of Israel" and of the state's Jewish identity ([Times of Israel, April 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/haredi-leaders-assail-oppressive-courts-order-to-sanction-draft-evaders/)). In September 2026, rallies welcomed about 160 men released from military prison; gift bags handed to children read "The welcoming ceremony for prisoners of the Torah" ([Ynet, September 2026](https://ynetnews.com/article/bydixytqzl)).

Yitzhak Goldknopf. United Torah Judaism chairman. Times of Israel. https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/haredi-leaders-assail-oppressive-courts-order-to-sanction-draft-evaders/. April 26, 2026
No sanction will stop the voice of the Torah.

The government's answer was the Bismuth bill, presented in November 2025. Its sponsors call it a draft law; critics call it an exemption bill. It set targets of 6,840 to 8,500 enlistees a year for four years, then "no less than 50 percent of the annual enlistment cohort", while letting full-time yeshiva students keep yearly deferrals to age 26 ([Times of Israel, November 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/bismuth-presents-bill-exempting-yeshiva-students-from-idf-draft-loosening-sanctions/)). IDI wrote that the October outline "does not establish an equal obligation for conscription" ([IDI, October 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61994)). The bill was shelved in March 2026, during the war with Iran ([VIN News, May 2026](https://vinnews.com/2026/05/17/haredi-parties-push-knesset-dissolution-as-draft-exemption-bill-returns-to-committee/)).

The draft split the coalition in its last year. Both factions of United Torah Judaism left the government over the stalled law in July 2025 ([Times of Israel, July 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/united-torah-judaism-quits-govt-to-protest-new-proposal-on-army-enlistment-exemptions/)), and the Knesset dissolved in July 2026, setting the vote for October 27, 2026. The Knesset was near the end of its four-year term anyway: the outgoing coalition "became the first Israeli government in decades to complete a full four-year term" ([JNS, July 2026](https://www.jns.org/news/israel-news/knesset-votes-to-dissolve-formally-sets-oct-27-election-date)). Money is part of the fight: after the 2024 ruling, NIS 480 million a year in yeshiva funding was revoked ([IDI, June 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/59892)); the wider question of coalition money for sectoral institutions is on [the economy page](/issues/economy).
What Israelis think

Among non-Haredi Jews, support for drafting Haredim rose from 67% in January 2024 to 84.5% in November 2024, and among national-religious respondents it doubled, from 36.5% to 72.5% ([IDI, December 2024](https://en.idi.org.il/press-releases/57753)). In the same survey, 74.5% of Likud voters and 79% of Religious Zionism voters supported it ([Times of Israel, December 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/survey-public-support-for-conscripting-ultra-orthodox-has-surged-throughout-war/)). Haredim were the exception: 61% wanted the current exemption kept and 20% supported some form of enlistment ([IDI, December 2024](https://en.idi.org.il/press-releases/57753)).

The burden behind that shift shows in reserve service. In 2025, 4.3% of religious men aged 21–44 were on reserve duty in an average month, against 1.7% of secular men and 0.3% of Haredi men ([IDI, August 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65427)).
<Chart id="haredi-draft.reserve" />

Agreement that Haredim should serve splits on who and how. In November 2025, Jewish Israelis divided between drafting everyone except outstanding yeshiva students (49.5%) and drafting only those not really studying (31%); about 75% of Haredim preferred the current system ([IDI, November 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/62072)).
<Chart id="haredi-draft.who-drafted" />

In July 2026, 46% of all Israelis said more pressure should be applied to enlist Haredi men, 31% conscription only with the agreement of Haredi leaders, and 11% called the effort futile. Likud voters preferred agreement, 75%; center and left voters preferred sanctions, 73% and 79%. Among Haredim, 45% chose agreement and 15% sanctions ([JPPI via Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-902297)). JPPI's published write-ups do not give the sample size. Questions differ across surveys: in June 2025, 41% of Jews chose universal conscription when offered several models, while 89% wanted the status quo changed ([INSS, June 2025](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/idf-conscription/)).

The issue moves some votes: 13.7% of Jews named a party's position on conscription as the biggest influence on their vote ([IDI, September 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/media/32364/august-voice-index-data.pdf)).
What the parties say
Most parties answered Ynet's September 2026 questionnaire on the draft; Likud declined. The two Haredi parties gave different answers on yeshiva dropouts.
<Positions issue="haredi-draft" />
Misreadings

**It is not a church-state fight.** An American reader may hear "religious exemption" and think of the First Amendment. The Israeli complaint is that one group does not carry a duty almost everyone else carries. National-religious Israelis, the most observant Zionists, became among the strongest supporters of drafting Haredim during 2024 ([IDI, December 2024](https://en.idi.org.il/press-releases/57753)), and religious men carry the highest reserve load ([IDI, August 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65427)).

**Haredim do serve, in growing numbers.** At least 4,000 enlisted in 2025–26, more than double the pre-war level ([Times of Israel, July 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/idf-chief-tells-haredi-commanders-army-must-grow-as-data-shows-uptick-in-enlistment/)), though that is "only slightly more than one-quarter of the estimated 14,000 haredim who reach draft age each year" ([Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-904035)). Few of the men who received draft orders reported: in the 2025 draft year, 701 of 15,938 whose dates had passed ([IDI, January 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63168)).

**The Haredi parties are not one bloc.** Shas accepted that dropouts can no longer be exempt; United Torah Judaism opposed drafting them ([Ynet, September 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/sjph72wyzx)). Only 28% of Haredim give their political leadership high marks ([IDI, August 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/65364)). More on the community is on [Haredim](/communities/haredim).

**The draft does not divide right from left.** People of Israel, which recommended Netanyahu before the vote, said it would not join a government that had not passed a draft law ([Jerusalem Post, September 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-907373)); Yisrael Beiteinu wants "no exemptions, no quotas and no deals" ([Ynet, September 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/sjph72wyzx)). Likud voters back drafting Haredim but prefer to do it by agreement ([JPPI via Jerusalem Post, July 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-902297)).

**The election was not called months early.** The draft ended the coalition, but only after it had become "the first Israeli government in decades to complete a full four-year term" ([JNS, July 2026](https://www.jns.org/news/israel-news/knesset-votes-to-dissolve-formally-sets-oct-27-election-date)).

**American communities are part of the story.** When the 2024 funding cut took effect, Rabbi Dov Landau, a dean of the Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak, "directly appealed to Haredim in the United States" for help, the Walla news site reported ([Times of Israel, April 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/the-high-courts-yeshiva-funding-ruling-goes-into-effect-today-what-does-it-mean/)).

documents.title: A Palestinian state and the 2026 vote

blocks.text: A Palestinian state and the 2026 vote
Where the lists that ran in the October 27, 2026 election stand on a Palestinian state, and what Israeli and Palestinian surveys show about the idea since 2013.
What is at stake

In Israel, left and right are defined mostly by positions on the Palestinians, the occupied territories and a Palestinian state, not by economics ([CHES-Israel expert survey, 2021–22](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/13540688231218917)). Yet in the 2026 campaign almost no one argued for a Palestinian state. Of the lists that ran in the October 27, 2026 election, only Ra'am and the Joint List say they support a Palestinian state ([Jerusalem Post, Sept 1, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-907154)). The Jewish-majority lists oppose one, say it is "not on the agenda", decline to answer, or, in the case of The Democrats, speak of "separation" ([Ynet party questionnaire, Sept 30, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/h1dpvu9cgl)).

The Knesset put this on record before the campaign began. On July 17, 2024 it passed, 68–9, a resolution stating that "the Knesset of Israel firmly opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state west of Jordan." Unlike a February 2024 resolution, which rejected only unilateral recognition, it rejected a state even as part of a negotiated settlement. Coalition parties were joined by members of Benny Gantz's National Unity; the nine votes against came from Ra'am and Hadash–Ta'al, and Yesh Atid and Labor left the chamber ([Times of Israel, July 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-overwhelmingly-against-palestinian-statehood-days-before-pms-us-trip/)). The Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, whose state is the question, are not Israeli citizens and had no vote in the October 27, 2026 election (see [who votes, and who doesn't](/how-it-works/who-votes)).

Since then, Knesset votes have been about annexation rather than partition. On July 23, 2025 a non-binding declaration in favor of annexing the West Bank and the Jordan Valley passed 71–13 ([Ynet, July 2025](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/bkxfw9algl)). On October 22, 2025 a bill by Noam's Avi Maoz to annex the settlement areas of the West Bank passed a preliminary reading 25–24 ([Times of Israel, Oct 22, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/rebelling-against-pm-mks-pass-preliminary-reading-of-west-bank-annexation-bill/)). The [West Bank page](/issues/west-bank) covers settlement and annexation in detail.

Abroad, the question moved the other way. By late September 2025, 157 of the 193 UN member states had recognized the State of Palestine, among them the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and France in September 2025 ([Al Jazeera, Sept 23, 2025](https://aljazeera.com/news/2025/9/23/which-are-the-150-countries-that-have-recognised-palestine-as-of-2025)). In Israel the recognitions united the main Jewish-majority parties rather than dividing them: Yair Lapid called it "a harmful step, and a reward for terror", Yair Golan called it "destructive", and Itamar Ben-Gvir called it "a prize for the murderous terrorists" ([Times of Israel, Sept 22, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-unites-against-hollow-palestine-recognition-but-pm-could-go-too-far/)).

When the Israel Democracy Institute asked voters to name their most important considerations, Jewish respondents chose foreign affairs and security (39%), the economy and cost of living (38%) and conscription (27%). The Palestinian issue was not offered as a separate answer ([IDI, Aug 31–Sept 3, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)). In the campaign, Netanyahu put the question this way:
Benjamin Netanyahu. Prime Minister, Likud. Jerusalem Post. https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-910068. Sept 18, 2026
Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?
What Israelis think

In 2026, 17% of Israelis and 16% of Jewish Israelis think Israel and a Palestinian state can coexist peacefully, down from 50% of all Israelis in 2013. For the first time in Pew's polling, more than half (56%) say coexistence is not possible ([Pew, Sept 15, 2026](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/15/many-israelis-and-palestinians-say-they-cannot-coexist-peacefully-and-explain-why/)). Pew says the share has not changed significantly from 21% in 2025. Pew's question asks about feasibility, not preference.
<Chart id="palestinian-state.pew-coexist" />

The chart above uses Pew's Global Attitudes series, which found that 37% of Jewish Israelis thought a way could be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully in spring 2014. Pew's separate survey of religion in Israel (fieldwork Oct 2014–May 2015, 5,601 adults) asked the same question and found 43% of Jewish Israelis ([Pew, March 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/comparisons-between-jews-in-israel-and-the-u-s/)). The samples are different. The [American lens page](/american-lens) cites the 43% figure.

In Pew's 2025 survey, 54% of Israelis on the left, 29% in the center and 7% on the right said a way can be found for Israel and a Palestinian state to coexist. Among Jewish Israelis, 25% of Hilonim (secular), 11% of Masortim (traditional) and 9% of Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) and Datiim (religious), counted together, said peaceful coexistence is possible ([Pew, Feb–March 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/06/pg_2025.06.03_israel_report.pdf)).

Tel Aviv University's Peace Index asks a different question: how far people support or oppose each of several outcomes. Among Jews, support for "the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside the State of Israel" fell from about 38% a month before October 7, 2023 (read from the Peace Index chart) to 23% in March 2026. Support for "annexation of the occupied territories and the creation of one state under Israeli rule with limited rights for Palestinians" rose from 30% to 38%, though in November 2025 half of Jews said they opposed it ([Peace Index, Nov 2025](https://en-social-sciences.tau.ac.il/sites/socsci-english.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/social/peaceindex/2025-11.pdf)). Whatever they prefer, 48% of Jews expect the current situation to continue ([Peace Index, March 2026](https://en-social-sciences.tau.ac.il/sites/socsci-english.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/social/peaceindex/2026-03.pdf)).
<Chart id="palestinian-state.peace-index-options" />
<Chart id="palestinian-state.peace-index-camps" />

The answers depend on the menu. When the Institute for National Security Studies offered a single choice that included "separation from the Palestinians", separation led among Jews at 32%, level with "full annexation without granting civil rights" at 31% ([INSS, June 16–22, 2026](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/inss-survey-june-2026/)).

Palestinian citizens of Israel are far more favorable. In the March 2026 Peace Index, 71% of Arab respondents supported a Palestinian state alongside Israel, from a small subsample of 103; in the INSS survey, 57% of Arab respondents chose two states. Their own first voting concern is crime in Arab society (53.5%) ([IDI, Sept 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66177)). The [Palestinian citizens page](/communities/palestinian-citizens) has more.

**What Palestinians think.** Pew asked the same question of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, its first survey there in several years; it could not survey in Gaza. 21% said a way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully and 68% said it cannot, against 17% and 56% of Israelis ([Pew, fieldwork March 30–April 28, 2026, 1,038 adults](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/15/many-israelis-and-palestinians-say-they-cannot-coexist-peacefully-and-explain-why/)). Asked why, they diverged. In Pew's summary, "While Israelis explain that an independent Palestinian state would pose a threat to Israel, many Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem say coexistence is not an option while they live under Israeli control." One Palestinian man told Pew: "They are an occupying force who took our land and separated us from each other with checkpoints."

The Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PCPSR) in Ramallah, which also interviews in Gaza, found in August 2026 that 44% supported and 50% opposed "the two-state solution" when it was offered without details, with almost the same support in the West Bank and Gaza. Offered three options, 56% chose "the two-state solution based on the 1967 borders" (52% in the West Bank, 61% in Gaza), 14% a confederation and 10% "one state in which Jews and Palestinians live with equal rights"; 58% said the two-state solution is no longer practical because of settlement expansion. Asked for the most effective way to end the occupation and establish a state, 44% chose negotiations, the highest share in four years, and 27% armed struggle, the lowest. Asked how Israeli policy toward Gaza and the West Bank would change if the Israeli opposition won and Netanyahu lost, 34% said it would not change, 33% said it would get worse and 28% better ([PCPSR, Aug 5–8, 2026, 1,270 adults: 830 in the West Bank, 440 in Gaza](https://www.pcpsr.org/en/node/1014)).

The last survey found that put the same questions to both publics, the Palestinian-Israeli Pulse (fieldwork July 17–29, 2024), found 40% of Palestinians and 21% of Jewish Israelis supporting a two-state solution; 6% of Palestinians and 10% of Jewish Israelis agreed that it is possible to trust the other side ([PCPSR and Tel Aviv University, July 2024](https://www.pcpsr.org/en/node/989)). No joint survey since then was found.
What the parties say
The table gives each list's answer in its own words, mostly from Ynet's questionnaire on the West Bank. Only Ra'am and the Joint List name a Palestinian state as a goal. Likud declined to answer.
<Positions issue="palestinian-state" />
Misreadings

**The election was not a referendum on two states.** No Jewish-majority list that ran in the October 27, 2026 election campaigned for a Palestinian state. Two of Netanyahu's leading opponents, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! and Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, answered Ynet that a state is "not on the agenda" and "We oppose a Palestinian state", respectively.

**Left and right do not mean what they mean in the United States.** As the CHES survey above found, Israel's left-right axis is the Palestinian question. Bennett and Eisenkot oppose Netanyahu but are not on the left on this question, and the Knesset's 68 votes against a state in 2024 included centrists from Gantz's party.

**Young Israelis are not the most dovish.** In the Palestinian-Israeli Pulse of December 2022, the latest age breakdown found, 20% of Jewish Israelis aged 18–34 backed the two-state solution in general, against 47% of those over 55 ([Pulse, TAU and PSR, Dec 2022](https://resolution.tau.ac.il/sites/socsci-english.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/resolution/Summary%20Report_%20English_Joint%20Poll%2024%20Jan%202023.pdf)).

**American Jews answer differently.** Asked Pew's same question before the war, 63% of American Jews thought a way could be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully ([Pew, fieldwork Nov 2019–June 2020](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/05/11/u-s-jews-connections-with-and-attitudes-toward-israel/)). The Israeli Jewish figure in 2026, from a different survey taken after the war began, is 16%; no Pew figure for American Jews on this question since 2020 was found.

No post-war survey of American Jews found for this page repeats the coexistence question. In February 2024 Pew asked a different one: 46% of American Jews said a two-state solution would be the best possible outcome ([Pew, Feb 13–25, 2024](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2024/03/21/majority-in-u-s-say-israel-has-valid-reasons-for-fighting-fewer-say-the-same-about-hamas/)).

**Opposing a state is not the same as backing annexation.** Among Jews, opposition to a Palestinian state is far larger than support for any single alternative. The status quo and separation draw large shares, and the outcome Jews most often expect, the current situation, is not the one they most often prefer.
Religion and state
Who controls marriage, conversion, kashrut, the Western Wall and religious funding in Israel, what the 25th Knesset changed, and what Israelis say they want.
What is at stake

Israel has no civil marriage. "Israel does not allow civil marriage, and Jewish marriages conducted in Israel must be sanctioned by Orthodox rabbis" ([Pew Research Center, March 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/israels-religiously-divided-society/)). All marriages must go through religious institutions, "such as the Chief Rabbinate for Jews" ([Times of Israel, March 7, 2023](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-must-recognize-online-marriages-conducted-via-utah-supreme-court-rules/)). Couples who cannot or will not marry that way go abroad: 9,550 couples registered civil marriages performed abroad in 2019. Since March 2023 they can also marry online through Utah, after the Supreme Court ordered the state to register those marriages; about 1,200 couples had done so since 2020 ([Times of Israel, March 7, 2023](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-must-recognize-online-marriages-conducted-via-utah-supreme-court-rules/)).
The 25th Knesset spent its last year expanding religious authority:

- **Child support.** In November 2025, 53–38, a two-year interim law let rabbinical courts rule on child support when both parties consent ([Times of Israel, Nov 17, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-expanding-rabbinical-courts-powers-to-arbitrate-civil-disputes/)).
- **Arbitration.** In March 2026, 65–41, rabbinical and Sharia courts gained the power to arbitrate civil money disputes when both sides sign consent ([VIN News, March 24, 2026](https://vinnews.com/2026/03/24/knesset-passes-rabbinic-courts-law-restoring-jurisdiction-over-arbitrated-monetary-matters/)).
- **Torah study.** In July 2026, 63–52, a Basic Law declared Torah study a "foundational value" of the state ([Times of Israel, July 14, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-contentious-basic-law-declaring-torah-study-a-constitutional-value/)). Its link to yeshiva exemptions is covered on the [draft page](/issues/haredi-draft).
- **Kashrut.** On July 15, 2026, 46–41, the Chief Rabbinate regained exclusive authority over kosher certification, reversing a reform that had let private Orthodox bodies certify ([Times of Israel, July 15, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-restoring-chief-rabbinates-monopoly-over-kosher-certification/)).
- **Gender segregation.** On July 16, 2026, 52–43, universities and colleges were allowed to run gender-segregated master's and doctoral programs ([Times of Israel, July 16, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-expanding-gender-segregation-in-academia/)).

Times of Israel reported that the kashrut law was part of a package in which the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties got the Torah study law and a freeze on draft arrests in exchange for backing other coalition bills. When the arbitration law passed, opposition leader Yair Lapid said this:
Yair Lapid. Opposition leader. VIN News. https://vinnews.com/2026/03/24/knesset-passes-rabbinic-courts-law-restoring-jurisdiction-over-arbitrated-monetary-matters/. March 24, 2026
Mark this day. Today is the day the status quo died—dead, buried, eliminated, canceled. It no longer exists and binds no one.

Money is the other half. The 2026 budget, passed 62–55 on March 30, raised funding for Haredi educational institutions from NIS 4.1 billion to NIS 5.17 billion ([Times of Israel, March 30, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-approves-2026-budget-israels-largest-ever-sending-billions-to-haredi-institutions/)). Separately, on March 10 the cabinet approved more than NIS 5 billion in coalition money for sectoral institutions. By a Berl Katznelson Center count, NIS 2.2 billion of it went to the Haredi community, including NIS 1.56 billion for yeshivas and kollels ([Times of Israel, March 10, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/cabinet-okays-1-6-billion-in-coalition-funds-including-715-million-for-ultra-orthodox/)). That money is covered on the [economy page](/issues/economy).

Conversion runs through the same institutions. On March 1, 2021, the Supreme Court ruled that conversions by the Reform and Conservative (Masorti) movements performed in Israel count for citizenship under the Law of Return. Eight of nine justices agreed on every point; the ninth wanted a 12-month delay. The court said the ruling had "no religious implications", and the movements say they perform "only 30 to 40 such conversions every year" in Israel ([Jerusalem Post, March 1, 2021](https://www.jpost.com/breaking-news/israel-to-recognize-reform-conservative-conversion-for-law-of-return-660592)). In May 2026, the ministerial legislation committee was set to vote on a bill by Religious Zionism MK Simcha Rothman amending the Law of Return to recognize only conversion "in accordance with halacha" ([Times of Israel, May 7, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ministerial-panel-to-vote-on-bill-that-would-bar-citizenship-for-non-orthodox-converts/)). Netanyahu asked the committee to postpone discussing it; the bill stayed on the agenda with no vote scheduled ([Jerusalem Post, May 12, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-895879)). No later report on it was found.

In January 2016 the government adopted the "Western Wall Compromise" (Decision 1075), which would have expanded the Wall's egalitarian section, Ezrat Yisrael, and made it formally regulated. In June 2017 it froze the compromise (Decision 2785) but told officials to keep developing the southern prayer plaza. In February 2026 the Supreme Court set "binding timetables" for accessibility work there, without changing arrangements at the main plaza ([IDI, Feb 25, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63581)). The Times of Israel described the bill below as "intended to undercut" that ruling ([Times of Israel, March 16, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-committee-advances-bill-expanding-orthodox-control-over-western-wall-plaza/)). Avi Maoz's bill would define "desecration" at Jewish holy sites as "conduct that contravenes the directives and rulings of the Chief Rabbinate." The Israel Democracy Institute wrote that the Rabbinate could then "issue a halakhic ruling" that stops Ezrat Yisrael "from continuing to operate" ([IDI, Feb 25, 2026](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63581)). JTA reported penalties of up to seven years in prison ([JTA, Feb 25, 2026](https://www.jta.org/2026/02/25/religion/bill-that-would-effectively-bar-egalitarian-prayer-at-the-western-wall-advances-in-israels-knesset)). It passed a preliminary reading in February 2026, 56–47 by the Jewish Chronicle's count; the Chronicle called it a first reading ([JC, Feb 26, 2026](https://www.thejc.com/news/israel/knesset-bill-orthodox-western-wall-mcambwxs)). Israeli Jews sort themselves on a scale of observance, not by denomination. In Central Bureau of Statistics data for 2025, Jews aged 20 and over defined themselves as 39.6% secular, 21.8% traditional but not particularly religious, 14.0% traditional-religious, 12.4% religious and 11.5% Haredi ([CBS via VIN News, Sept 2026](https://vinnews.com/2026/09/09/israel-enters-5787-with-population-growth-high-birthrate-and-rising-emigration/)).

Misreadings

**"Reform versus Orthodox" is the American fault line, not the Israeli one.** In Pew's 2014–15 survey, 3% of Israeli Jews identified as Reform and 2% as Conservative, against 35% and 18% of American Jews in Pew's 2013 U.S. survey ([Pew Research Center, March 2016](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/03/08/comparisons-between-jews-in-israel-and-the-u-s/)). Half of Israeli Jews (50%) named Orthodoxy as the stream they identify with, and 41% named none. The Israeli divide runs from secular through traditional to religious and Haredi. The movements still have a voice in the Knesset. Gilad Kariv, a Democrats MK and "an ordained Reform rabbi" ([Times of Israel, May 7, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ministerial-panel-to-vote-on-bill-that-would-bar-citizenship-for-non-orthodox-converts/)), placed third on the party's list in its July 20, 2026 primary, behind Yair Golan and Naama Lazimi ([Arutz Sheva, July 20, 2026](https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/430471)). He said the conversion bill would "collapse the bridge between the State of Israel and Jews around the world" ([Times of Israel, May 7, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ministerial-panel-to-vote-on-bill-that-would-bar-citizenship-for-non-orthodox-converts/)). No other Reform or Conservative rabbi on a 2026 list was confirmed for this page.

**Support for civil marriage is not a demand for a wall between synagogue and state.** In a July 2025 poll of Jews commissioned by Hiddush, a group that campaigns for marriage freedom, 53% said they would choose an Orthodox marriage "if all options were legally equal" ([Jerusalem Post, Aug 2025](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-863596)). The state already funds Haredi schools and legislates the powers of rabbinical and Sharia courts, as the laws above show. The argument is over who controls religious institutions and how much they get, not whether the state is involved at all.

**Diaspora causes rank low with Israeli voters, but they are on the agenda.** The Western Wall dominates American Jewish coverage. In Israel, in the last measure found (IDI, 2019), 15.5% of Jews called religion and state "extremely important" to their vote, and egalitarian prayer at the Wall had bare-majority support. Still, bills on the Wall and on non-Orthodox conversion both came up in the 2026 Knesset, as described above.

**Majorities do not make policy here.** Majorities of Jews back civil marriage and Shabbat buses, yet the 25th Knesset expanded religious authority. The IDI figures above show who puts these issues first: most Haredim, and few other Jews. The Torah study and kashrut laws were part of the coalition deal described above.

**It is not only a Jewish issue.** The 2026 arbitration law covers Sharia courts as well as rabbinical ones. Arab respondents to JPPI's May 2026 survey opposed a civil marriage option, 46% to 39%. For more, see [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens).
The war and the hostages
Where the Gaza war, the Iran and Lebanon fronts and the Oct 7 inquiry stood in September 2026, what Israelis think about them, and what the parties promise.
What is at stake

The Gaza war (officially in Israel, "Swords of Iron") began on October 7, 2023, when Hamas-led gunmen attacked southern Israel, killing some 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 hostages ([Times of Israel, Oct 10, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/gaza-ceasefire-starts-as-idf-completes-partial-withdrawal-hamas-has-72-hours-to-return-hostages/)); 1,200 is the Israeli Foreign Ministry's count, revised from 1,400 ([Nov 10, 2023](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-november-10-2023/)). A UN team led by Pramila Patten, the UN's special representative on sexual violence in conflict, found "reasonable grounds to believe that conflict-related sexual violence occurred in multiple locations," including rape and gang rape in at least three, though it could not verify reported rapes in some; it found "clear and convincing information" of rape and sexualized torture of hostages ([UN News, March 4, 2024](https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/03/1147217)).

Three years on, the rescue question is closed. All 251 people abducted that day have come home: 166 alive and 85 dead, of whom 41 were taken alive and killed in captivity ([Times of Israel, Oct 3, 2026](https://timesofisrael.com/ex-hostage-point-man-says-israel-could-have-returned-all-oct-7-captives-a-year-earlier)). The live arguments are whether they could have come home sooner, and who investigates Oct 7. Nitzan Alon, the IDF's former hostage point man, said in October 2026 that Israel "could and should have shortened the war" and brought the captives home "maybe a year earlier," and that Netanyahu "also had his political and personal considerations."

**Gaza.** A ceasefire under a US-brokered deal took effect on October 10, 2025 ([Times of Israel, Oct 10, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/gaza-ceasefire-starts-as-idf-completes-partial-withdrawal-hamas-has-72-hours-to-return-hostages/)). The share of Gaza that Israel occupies grew from about 53% at the ceasefire to nearly 70% by August 2026 ([Chatham House, Aug 3, 2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/08/agreeing-disarm-hamas-trying-call-israels-bluff-gaza)), and Israel has carried out "near-daily strikes throughout Gaza since the ceasefire" ([Times of Israel, May 5, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/board-of-peace-wont-hold-israel-to-truce-terms-if-hamas-doesnt-okay-disarmament-offer/)). The Gaza Health Ministry counts 73,922 Palestinians killed since October 2023, 1,402 of them since the ceasefire was announced. OCHA attributes these figures to the ministry, which "operates under the de facto authorities" ([UN OCHA, Sept 23](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/reported-impact-snapshot-gaza-strip-23-september-2026) and [Sept 25, 2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026)).
Saad Abu Aita, 49, lives in a tent in central Gaza and awaits medical evacuation abroad:

Each side accuses the other of breaking the truce. The IDF said gunmen from a tunnel in Rafah killed two soldiers on October 19, 2025, a Hamas "violation"; Israeli strikes that day killed at least 45 people, Gaza's Hamas-run civil defense said ([Times of Israel, Oct 19, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-october-19-2025/)).

**Iran and Lebanon.** Announcing the Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire that took effect on November 27, 2024, President Biden said Hezbollah's cross-border attacks had forced 70,000 Israelis to flee their homes in the north ([Times of Israel, Nov 26, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-november-26-2024/)). Iran attacked Israel directly in April and October 2024 ([Apr 14](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-april-14-2024/), [Oct 2, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-october-2-2024/)); Israel struck Iran on June 13, 2025, and the two exchanged fire until a ceasefire on June 24 ([June 24, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-june-24-2025/)). The US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, 2026 ([Feb 28, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-february-28-2026/)), and on September 1 US forces struck Revolutionary Guard targets in Iran ([Sept 1, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-september-1-2026/)). Israeli troops were still in southern Lebanon in late September ([Times of Israel, Sept 28, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-september-28-2026/)).

**The cost at home.** Since October 7, 2023, 1,318 security personnel have been added to the official fallen roll, the [Defense Ministry reported](https://www.mod.gov.il/כתבות-ומבזקים/חדשות-משרד-הביטחון/שלוש-שנים-למלחמת-התקומה) on October 4, 2026; the National Insurance Institute counts 1,029 civilians killed in terrorist attacks, [JNS reported](https://www.jns.org/news/israel-news/israel-marks-1-318-slain-security-personnel-since-oct-7). Both totals include October 7. The IDF promised to cap reserve duty at 70 days in 2026; by late September "most reserve units have already exceeded 100 days" ([Jerusalem Post, Sept 25, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/defense-news/article-909671)). How the load falls by community is on [the draft page](/issues/haredi-draft).

**The inquiry.** A state commission of inquiry under the 1968 law has its members appointed by the Supreme Court president and must be headed by a judge ([IDI, Dec 24, 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/62785)). Netanyahu opposes one. His coalition's alternative, described as a "national" commission, has no judges choosing its members: 80 Knesset members would appoint it, or else coalition and opposition would name three each. It passed a first reading 59–0 on July 6, 2026, with the opposition boycotting ([Times of Israel, July 7, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-controversial-politically-appointed-oct-7-probe-in-1st-reading/)), and was not completed before the end of the Knesset term ([Ynet, Oct 4, 2026](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/r1sz8wyimx)). On September 23 the Supreme Court left the decision to the next government, which must respond by January 15, 2027 ([Times of Israel, Sept 23, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/high-court-delays-decision-on-october-7-state-commission-until-after-election/)).

Misreadings

**"The Israeli argument is the American one."** An American reader may expect the argument to center on Palestinian civilians. In Israel the mainstream argument was hostages against fighting on, and now it is accountability. In July 2025, 78% of Jews said Israel is "making substantial efforts to avoid causing unnecessary suffering to Palestinians in Gaza"; 22.5% of Arab citizens agreed. In the same survey, asked "To what extent are you personally troubled or not troubled by the reports of famine and suffering among the Palestinian population in Gaza?", 79% of Jews said they were not so troubled or not at all troubled; 86% of Arab citizens said they were troubled ([IDI, July 2025](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/60357)). Some Jewish Israelis dissented in the hostages' name. In April 2025 close to 1,000 Air Force veterans signed a letter demanding the hostages' return even if it meant ending the war; over 150 former navy officers wrote that "the resumption of fighting delays the release of the hostages, endangers the soldiers and harms innocent civilians" ([Times of Israel, Apr 10, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog-april-10-2025/)). Views closer to American critics' are held mainly by [Palestinian citizens of Israel](/communities/palestinian-citizens), 93% of whom wanted the war ended in September 2025 ([IDI](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/61845)).

**"The war is over."** Gaza has a ceasefire, but Israel held nearly 70% of the Strip in August 2026 and struck it near-daily; the Gaza Health Ministry counts 1,402 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire was announced. Troops stayed in southern Lebanon into late September.

**"The hostage families were one movement."** In June 2025 the Hostages and Missing Families Forum called "the return of all hostages through a comprehensive deal" "the victory of this war" ([Times of Israel, June 22, 2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/hostage-forum-welcomes-return-of-slain-captives-urges-government-to-use-iran-momentum-for-deal-to-free-all-hostages/)). The Tikva Forum, another group of hostage families, seeks every captive's release "by means which strengthen the State of Israel," and says "our only option is to win this war" ([Tikva Forum](https://tikva-leumit.org.il/en/eng/)).
**"The inquiry is a side issue."** It is also a fight about judges: whether the Supreme Court president picks the panel. See [courts and the judicial overhaul](/issues/courts).
The West Bank and annexation
How Israel has extended its rule over the West Bank since 2023, mostly through planning and administration rather than law, and where Israelis and the parties stand.
What is at stake

The West Bank is the land between Israel and Jordan that Israel captured in 1967 and has held under military occupation since. "Occupied" is the term used by the UN, whose humanitarian office reports on the "occupied Palestinian territory," by the European Union, whose annual report is titled [2025 Report on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/2025%20Report%20on%20Israeli%20settlements%20in%20the%20occupied%20West%20Bank.pdf), and by the International Court of Justice, whose non-binding 2024 advisory opinion refers to "the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967" ([Times of Israel, July 19, 2024](https://www.timesofisrael.com/world-court-israeli-presence-in-east-jerusalem-west-bank-is-illegal-and-must-end/)); this site uses it too. Israel's government rejects the label and calls the territory "disputed," arguing that its hold on the West Bank cannot be considered an occupation "both because the territory historically belonged to ancient Israel and because it captured the territory from Jordan, which had no legal claim to it" ([Jerusalem Post, July 2023](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-752919)). Netanyahu answered the court: "The Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land" (same Times of Israel report).

The 1995 Oslo II agreement, meant to last five years, split the territory into three zones that are still in force: Area A, the Palestinian cities (about 18%), under the Palestinian Authority; Area B (about 22%), under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control; and Area C (about 60%), under full Israeli control ([B'Tselem](https://www.btselem.org/area_c/what_is_area_c)). More than 3 million people live in the West Bank, 85% of them Palestinian (end of 2023, [Peace Now](https://peacenow.org.il/en/settlements-watch/settlements-data/population)). The Palestinians among them live under Israeli military rule, are not Israeli citizens and had no vote in the October 27, 2026 election; the Israeli settlers living beside them do (see [who votes, and who doesn't](/how-it-works/who-votes)). The two groups also live under different law: the International Court of Justice found that "Palestinians in the West Bank are thus subject to military law and military courts, whereas settlers benefit from the criminal law and criminal justice system applicable to civilians in Israel" ([ICJ, July 19, 2024, para. 136](https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=A/78/968&l=en&t=pdf)).

How many settlers there are depends on East Jerusalem: the EU counts its Israeli neighborhoods as settlements, while Israel does not. Without East Jerusalem, 541,085 Jews lived in the West Bank on Jan 1, 2026 ([JNS](https://www.jns.org/exclusive-judea-samaria-jewish-population-grew-at-twice-israels-overall-rate-in-2025/)). With it, the EU counts over 750,000 Israeli settlers, 15% of the West Bank's population, East Jerusalem included ([EU, 2025 report](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/2025%20Report%20on%20Israeli%20settlements%20in%20the%20occupied%20West%20Bank.pdf)). The two figures differ in source, group counted and date, so their gap is not an exact count of East Jerusalem's settlers. The settlements include Haredi cities in the West Bank, such as Modi'in Illit and Beitar Illit, whose residents are Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) and are counted in these totals; they are covered on the [Haredim page](/communities/haredim) and the [settlers page](/communities/settlers).

"Annexation" means applying Israeli law and administration to this land. Israel's right calls it "applying sovereignty." The Knesset has not passed it into law. A July 2025 Knesset motion calling the West Bank an "inseparable part of the Land of Israel" passed 71–13 and has no legal force ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-71-13-for-non-binding-motion-calling-to-annex-west-bank/)). On Oct 22, 2025, two bills passed a preliminary reading, one applying Israeli law to "all areas of settlement" ([Jerusalem Post](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-871299)) 25–24 and one for Ma'ale Adumim 32–9 ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/israel-west-bank-annexation-bills-trump-objection-vance-visit/)). Netanyahu told Likud MKs to abstain. No later vote on either bill was found before the Knesset dissolved in July 2026. Trump had already ruled annexation out in September 2025:

The larger change has come through administration. In 2023 Bezalel Smotrich set up a Settlement Administration inside the Defense Ministry. On May 29, 2024, the army's Central Command delegated Civil Administration powers over land, planning and registration to a civilian deputy ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/drawing-annexation-claims-idf-hands-many-west-bank-powers-to-civilian-ally-of-smotrich/)). In February 2026 the cabinet eased Israeli purchase of private land, extended oversight into Areas A and B, and opened land registration in Area C. The Foreign Ministry called this "an administrative measure"; Smotrich called it part of "the normalization and de facto sovereignty revolution that we are leading" ([Times of Israel, Feb 19, 2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/expansion-of-west-bank-rule-appears-to-shift-creeping-annexation-into-higher-gear/)).

Settlement planning reached records. In 2025, 54 new settlements were approved and 86 outposts set up, 58 of them "agricultural farms" (Peace Now, [2025 summary](https://peacenow.org.il/en/summary-of-2025-in-settlements)).

A tender for 1,234 of them was due to close on Oct 19, 2026, eight days before the vote ([Peace Now, Aug 2026](https://peacenow.org.il/en/e1-tender-published-and-open-for-bidding)).

Settler violence has also risen. UN OCHA counted 1,189 settler attacks causing Palestinian casualties or property damage in 2023, 1,420 in 2024 and 1,828 in 2025, the highest since its count began in 2006 (OCHA via the [EU report](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/2025%20Report%20on%20Israeli%20settlements%20in%20the%20occupied%20West%20Bank.pdf)). Of the police investigation files on ideologically motivated offenses by Israelis against Palestinians that Yesh Din has monitored since 2005, 93.6% ended without an indictment ([Yesh Din](https://www.yesh-din.org/en/data-sheet-law-enforcement-on-israeli-civilians-in-the-west-bank-settler-violence-2005-2025/), Jan 2026).

OCHA counts deaths in both directions: Palestinians and Israelis killed or injured "in the context of the occupation and conflict," each incident "validated by at least two independent and reliable sources." It counts as a civilian "whoever is neither a member of security forces (including police) nor fulfills a combat function within an armed group" ([OCHA](https://www.ochaopt.org/data/casualties)). In 2025, by its count, Israeli forces killed 225 Palestinians in the West Bank and settlers killed nine; for six more it is unknown whether forces or settlers killed them. Of the 240, 55 were children. Palestinians killed 17 Israelis in the West Bank, one of them a child and six of them members of Israeli forces, and attacks by Palestinians from the West Bank killed three Israelis inside Israel ([OCHA, Jan 7, 2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-352-west-bank)).

The IDF counts "nationalistic" Jewish incidents differently: 1,045 in 2023, 682 in 2024 and 867 in 2025 ([Jerusalem Post, Jan 19, 2026](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-883857)). OCHA's count rises every year; the IDF's falls in 2024 before rising again. INSS, using defense-establishment data, counts 660 "nationalist crime" incidents in the first half of 2026, up 63% on the previous half-year ([INSS, Sept 2026](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/jewish-terror-alert/)).

In June 2026, INSS found three camps of about a quarter each: separation from the Palestinians, a two-state solution, and full annexation without civil rights for Palestinians ([INSS, June 2026](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/inss-survey-june-2026/)). The divide runs between the blocs: half of coalition voters chose annexation, while opposition voters split between separation (40%) and two states (36%). Misreadings

**"Annexation" is not mostly a Knesset vote.** The bills are symbolic or stalled. The change has come through planning approvals, the 2024 delegation order and the 2026 land decisions, which Smotrich himself describes as de facto sovereignty.

**"Separation" is not "two states."** Without the map of Areas A, B and C, "sovereignty over Area C" sounds like annexing everything, and the Democrats' "separation" sounds like a Palestinian state. They are different plans.

**The blocs do not line up with the positions.** Two lists running against Netanyahu, B'Yachad and Yisrael Beiteinu, back annexing Area C, and Yisrael Beiteinu backs building in E1. The Haredi parties, Netanyahu's allies, do not make the issue central to their campaigns, Ynet reports.

**The terms are positions.** The biblical name used in most of the party statements above or "West Bank," "sovereignty" or "annexation," "farms" or "outposts," "nationalist crime," "Jewish terror" or "settler violence": each word signals where its speaker stands.
